Madison Humphrey is sharing a message of self-care after returning home from the hospital in time for Thanksgiving.

“I just wanted to say thank you so much for all the kind messages checking in,” Humphrey, 27, wrote via her Instagram Story on Thursday, November 26, one day after she was rushed to the emergency room.

The influencer — who is best known for her “Divorced Mom” and “Leasing Manager” sketches — added that she was “super thankful to be home resting and on the mend!”.

Humphrey posted a photo of herself holding what appeared to be get-well-soon flowers in the kitchen, as she reminded her followers to take care of themselves amid cold and flu season.

“There’s a lot going around this year so a good reminder to stay mindful, rested and hydrated,” she wrote, but didn’t give any more details about her condition.

According to recent reports, the TikToker did, however, joke, “And yes I did (finally) get to finish DWTS! Congratulations to Erza [Frech] and Daniella [Karagach] on their beautiful win!!” referring to the Tuesday, November 24, season 35 finale of the dance competition.

“Wishing everyone a wonderful Thanksgiving today,” she concluded.

Humphrey’s upbeat message came one day after she informed her followers that she was in the hospital.

“One minute you’re watching the Dancing With the Stars finale and the next, being rushed to the ER,” Humphrey wrote via her Instagram Story on Wednesday, November 25.

She posted a picture lying in a hospital bed, wearing sweatpants, a T-shirt and Ugg boots while being hooked up to a monitor.

While Humphrey didn’t give any more information about what happened, she thanked the “incredible medical staff who work holidays, nights, days and long hours to keep us all safe and healthy.”.

Humphrey is a content creator who is known for her comedic sketches and parody videos on TikTok, many of which have been pegged to Dancing With the Stars.

She has amassed five million followers on TikTok and was named one of the 10 creators in the Icon category for the platform’s 2026 The Discover List.

Last month, Humphrey declared that her leasing manager character was getting made into a TV show with Tubi, taking her comedic chops to the next level.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

In a recent development, the SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple claims the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

It has been revealed that if your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

It has been revealed that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Recent findings suggest that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one last month of 2026 brings two more waves of Xbox Game Pass titles to close out the year. Subscribers can once again look forward to some latest arrivals in the Xbox Game Pass library, ranging from gruesome co-op action to wholesome adventures featuring helpful mice on a mission. These announcements typically come in two waves, with a sneak peek split between them, so while this list isn’t complete yet, we do know what you can expect in the first half of December. As usual, we’ll revision this page once Xbox reveals the full lineup for this first batch. For now, you can look forward to an eclectic mix of games, starting with The Outlast Trials. Released in 2024, it’s a co-op survival-horror game that throws a team of up to four players into a gauntlet of deadly trials, where evasion is key to victory. You can also play it solo, and if the onslaught of festive season cheerfulness is getting to you, then this will be a nice–but brutal–change of pace. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hCgiwsIUI4g If you’d prefer to focus on the coziness of the season, then Hela: Of Mice and Magic looks like a fun time. Set in a magical forest inspired by Scandinavian lands, the game follows a group of mice on a journey to help people, at the behest of an old witch who can’t make the trip herself. This is also a day-one release for Xbox Game Pass, and it’ll be joined by World of Tanks Blitz on the same day. On December 3, Freestyle Football 2 launches, bringing fast-paced, 5v5 multiplayer street soccer to Xbox and PC, and on December 14, you can grab Nubby’s Number Factory, a roguelite game all about making substantial numbers. Xbox Game Pass December Wave 1 Games December 1 The Outlast Trials (Cloud, Xbox Series X|S, and PC) — Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium, PC Game Pass Hela: Of Mice and Magic (Cloud, Xbox Series X|S, and PC) — Game Pass Ultimate, PC Game Pass World of Tanks Blitz December 3 Freestyle Football 2 December 14 Nubby’s Number Factory If you missed it, November brought a solid selection of releases. The first wave added the dungeon-crawling roguelike deck-building game Dungeon Crawlers to more Game Pass tiers, along with Warhammer Survivors and John Carpenter’s Toxic Commando. The Game Pass library expanded further later in November, with some Paw Patrol fun for the kiddos, High on Life 2, and the pretty good long-distance stealth game Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts 2.

Breaking: The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Doubles Down On A Once Upon A Time In Hollywood Controversy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".
  • It simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself.
  • Recent findings suggest that that quickly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

It simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself. After wowing audiences everywhere in 2019 with "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the quirky and uber-talented filmmaker returned to the scene of the crime (so to speak) once more with his long-awaited sequel/spin-off film, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." This time, the buddy comedy act with Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton and Brad Pitt's Cliff has been dropped, focusing solely on the latter as the stuntman embarks on his latest round of mischief. Though Tarantino stepped aside from his directing duties to make room for David Fincher, well, let's just say that the script is as purely QT as it gets.

Recent findings suggest that that quickly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before. You see, despite so much acclaim from critics and fans alike, "Once Upon a Time" drew the ire of many with its irreverent treatment of martial arts legend Bruce Lee, portrayed by Mike Moh in the film. Even Lee's family weighed in on the matter, objecting to how easily Cliff puts the arrogant Lee in his place during a fight scene on the set of a film. Not surprisingly, "Cliff Booth" returns to this fraught topic on several occasions, and it certainly feels like a meta-textual jab at the real-world backlash from before.

Sources indicate that was this in poor taste, or is Tarantino merely poking fun with a self-deprecating running joke? Moviegoers will undoubtedly have strong takes on either side. Here's where we land on our second go-around with this little debate.

You know, there's something to be stated for addressing an uncomfortable matter head-on instead of dancing around it — or even ignoring it altogether. Quentin Tarantino has never been one to shy away from a fight, a trait he happens to share with washed-up stuntman Cliff Booth. As a master cinephile, a brilliant bartender, a hit with the ladies, and a ruthless killer all in one, the power fantasy of it all isn't exactly hard to see in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Perhaps that's what made the Bruce Lee moment in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" stand out all the more (a fight that almost ended very differently). It's one thing for Cliff to be the coolest person alive in his world, and quite another for him to intrude rudely upon our own.

So how does "Cliff Booth" address this elephant in the room? Although the incident is brought up on a number of occasions in passing, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II's buzzy actor Rodrick "Hot Rod" Harrison is positively fixated on it once he meets Cliff — a fact that also seems to catch the eye of talent manager Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki). Intriguingly, Cliff himself almost seems embarrassed by the attention, perhaps self-reflexively brushing it off as the brash actions of a young man. Maybe, like Tarantino himself, he's a little older and a little wiser and less apt to repeat the same mistakes.

Industry observers note that less generously, the fact that this fight is emphasized so much in "Cliff Booth" could make the exact opposite point. It's treated almost like a legend or a myth in this world, giving Cliff a dangerous sense of aura and mystique that belies his charming appearance.

In a recent development, either way, this is just one ingredient tossed into a much larger stew. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may struggle to reach the transcendent heights of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," but isn't that part of its point, too? "What is Cliff Booth without Rick Dalton?" Quentin Tarantino's script seems to be asking. Not dissimilarly, is a Tarantino movie with David Fincher at the wheel really a Tarantino movie anymore? Who can say how much ownership any of us have over our own art — or our lives in general?

In a recent development, perhaps that's why "Cliff Booth" feels so much colder and mean-spirited than its predecessor. Although both films build to violent climaxes, the one in "Hollywood" is shot to be much more over-the-top and darkly funny than the one here. Before, Rick Dalton and Cliff were fighting to preserve a very specific way of life — one that the Manson family threatened to overturn. Here, Cliff very easily could've avoided the bloodshed with killers Eddie (Matt Groove) and Fernando Verdusco (JB Tadena), but he pursues this anyway out of ... ego? Principle? A sense of right and wrong? Cliff is a man of both simplicity and contradictions, so perhaps it's only fitting that the filmmaking style reflects this through Fincher's very different approach, as well.

Industry observers note that that's where the repeated jabs about the Bruce Lee fight come in, as a moment that Cliff has no choice but to own. "Cliff Booth" is a movie about our attempts to define our own stories — whether it be himself, the troublemaking TV star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), or Karen. And maybe Bruce Lee, too.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is now playing in limited theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that even if you haven't read any of the books, you've probably heard of Dungeon Crawler Carl at this point. The LitRPG book series (a genre defined by its use of video game and tabletop RPG mechanics) by Matt Dinniman has become a cultural juggernaut, and it is only getting bigger. In addition to a television adaptation, Dungeon Crawler Carl is also getting another new adaptation in 2027.

Vault Comics will be publishing an ongoing Dungeon Crawler Carl comic. The new comic will serialize the existing webtoon adaptation of Dungeon Crawler Carl, retaining writer Tevagah with artwork by Laurel Pursuit Studios. Kuzomari will also join the series to help adapt the art to the larger comic-book format. Nathan Gooden will provide the main covers, with plenty of variants also being made available.

For the uninitiated, this is the official synopsis for the series:.

According to recent reports, dungeon Crawler Carl follows Coast Guard vet Carl and his ex-girlfriend’s cat, Princess Donut, as they try to survive the end of the world — or just get to the next level — in a video game-like, trap-filled fantasy dungeon. A dungeon that’s actually the set of a reality television show with countless viewers across the galaxy.

On the latest adaptation of his novels, Dinniman said, "Entering the comic space is nothing short of amazing. The fact that I get to work with some of the greatest creators and artists working today feels like a dream.”.

The first concern of the Dungeon Crawler Carl comic will be a double-sized, 48-page affair and is set to be released in January 2027.

We know Dinniman is actively working on the ninth book in the series, though there is no release date as of yet. It is right now being called The Beautiful Place, and the author has even shared the prologue and early chapters. The most recent book in the series was released this year, and if Dinniman writes at his usual pace, it wouldn't be unsurprising to see the ninth book release sometime in late 2027. Dinniman has remarked this will begin the conclusion to the series, which should end with the tenth book.

According to recent reports, beyond the main series, a lot of Dungeon Crawler Carl projects are still in the works. During Latest York Comic Con, Universal Global Television scripted series chief Kelsey Balance revealed that shooting could begin as early as next year. Dungeon Crawler Carl also has a pretty solid tabletop RPG.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kerry Kennedy is not in Milan on political business, but it’s hard to rein in the enthusiasm of some Americans following the 2026 midterm elections. Democrats won decisive majorities in both the House and Senate, along with 24 of the 36 governors elections held this month. It was a blue tsunami. Kennedy—a lawyer and human rights activist born in 1959 to dynasty Democrats Robert and Ethel Kennedy—is in a celebratory mood.

She’s in town for one night only to attend a charity dinner in support of her foundation, the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center. But first she sits down with Vanity Fair Italia, and over the course of our chat, she takes her beloved poodle, Scamper, for a short walk; sips two cappuccinos (strictly decaf), one of them iced (she apologizes to the Italians present); eats some gianduiotti chocolates; gestures animatedly; and smooths her very blonde hair.

But above all, she never stops smiling: “In America you can only go so far in the attempt to avoid the rule of law and erode democracy,” she says, making clear that her political statements are delivered in her personal capacity, “because at a certain point, even if you’re the most powerful and the richest man there, democracy will bring you down. [The president] made a mess all over the world, but in the end, in America, democracy was stronger.”.

From left: Robert Kennedy Jr., Joseph P Kennedy Jr., Tory Kennedy, and Kerry Kennedy on January 1, 1994.

Vanity Fair: What do voters want today?

Kerry Kennedy: They’re upset about high prices. And they don’t like the corruption.

What do you think will happen to Donald Trump and his associates?

I think that [Representative] Jamie Raskin is now going to be the head of the Judiciary Committee. I happen to know him very, very, very well because Jamie and I studied for the bar together. He’s brilliant, he’s determined, and he hates anything that harms our Constitution. I think that Trump is going to face impeachment. The rumors are that Trump’s going to fire [Pete] Hegseth, but if he isn’t fired, he’ll certainly be impeached.

What will be the repercussions of the blue tsunami for Tehran?

It has been revealed that iran’s leader at the moment, [Mojtaba Khamenei], has seen his father murdered by Trump. His head of state was murdered by Trump. His spiritual leader was murdered by Trump. Now Trump wants to make a peace deal with this guy. The only way to make progress is for the Iranians to think that it’s not Trump but someone else who’s negotiating.

The fact that Donald Trump sold out Western values in Ukraine for a barrel of oil from a mad, thieving, murderous dictator in Russia shocked the American people and shocked people around the world. Congress has the power of the purse, and now it’s going to exercise that power. But….

He’s still the president for two more years. We didn’t get the White House.

Ethel Kennedy and daughter Kerry Kennedy circa 1979.

Who is your ideal candidate for the 2028 presidential election?

Anyone whose last name is Democrat.

Do you think [President Barack] Obama played a role in the Democrats’ success?

Obama is beloved. The only person who’s beloved more is Michelle [Obama]. And when I watched his speeches, he was so clear and concise about the differences between the Republicans and the Democrats, with his moral authority and his joy.

You’ve talked about how your mother supported your father. Can you share an example of that?

Industry observers note that my father was working for the Senate, and he was investigating organized crime’s infiltration of the Teamsters union, stealing pension funds from the rank-and-file Teamsters. There was a journalist from the Latest York Post who was also investigating, and somebody threw acid in his face. He was permanently blinded. A few days later, my mother got an anonymous letter saying, “Your children will be next.” She took her three oldest kids, put them in the back of her car, drove them to the Capitol, walked into the hearing room, and sat in the front row while daddy was interrogating Jimmy Hoffa, the head of the Teamsters.

It has been revealed that she was saying, “You’re not going to get to me through my children, and you’re not going to get to my husband through me. We are a fortress and we’re coming after you.” I don’t know how she grappled with the trauma.

She probably did it for her children.

It has been revealed that she needed to be there for us. She was an athlete. And if you feel physically mighty, it’s very helpful when you have to also be psychologically mighty. She would get up and go swimming, then horseback riding, sailing, and after a sail, she would go for a swim. She also had a very deep faith. She went to Mass every day, prayed before and after every meal, and she made us read the Bible out loud at the dinner table every night.

Yes. In December, I’ll step down from being president of this organization. I’ll stay on the board and I’ll be president emeritus and I’ll still be involved, but I want to go to divinity school.

Stephen Colbert and Kerry Kennedy on December 11, 2013.

I don’t know. I have to apply and be accepted.

In 2008 you wrote the bestseller Being Catholic Now. What does it mean to be Catholic in 2026?

Recent findings suggest that for Americans, we have had this extremely disruptive, terrifying time for the last two years, and there are existential threats that everybody in the world is facing. And suddenly there’s an American pope who’s saying, “When you feel this is wrong, it is wrong. When this president is allowing ICE agents to go into American cities and start shooting people, that’s wrong. We need to have compassion toward one another. We need to have love toward one another. Every human being is valuable.”.

He’s one of the few voices—not one Republican senator has stood up, and other leaders around the world really have not stood up. Mark Carney did from Canada.

Pedro Sánchez [Spain’s prime minister] did a little bit.

Yes, but not much. The pope has been the main person, and I think that’s renewed people’s faith because it’s very simple as a political leader to call on people’s anger and hatred and fury. It’s a simple trick to get elected. But what people really want you to do in the end is call upon their better angels and say, “You’re good. I see that the God in me sees the God in you.” That is the alternative message, and that’s the spiritual message. I think that it’s created a revival of faith. My daughter Cara is 31 years old, and every Sunday night, she and all of her friends go to church and it’s packed.

What lesson did you learn from your parents?

When we were kids, when we would have a battle, and there were lots of battles, my father always did the same thing. He would bring two of us into a room. My brother had to be silent, and I would tell my father what happened and all the horrible things my brother did. And then I’d have to be silent, and he would tell his story. And then it would be clear that neither of us was completely innocent. We would have to kiss and make up and go to our rooms to read for an hour. His message to us was his message to our country, which is: You have to stop thinking of your adversary as your enemy and think of them as your brother and sister.

Your brother, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., right now the secretary of health in the Trump administration, is known for his anti-vax views. You’ve often mentioned, “I love him very much, but I don’t agree with him.”.

We were very close, but he changed and went way over there. And that’s where he is today. But we have much more in common than not.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr and Kerry Kennedy on May 20, 2015.

I’m not going to go talk to him about vaccine policy. That’s not going to change him, and he’s not going to change me. So when I’m with him, I want to talk about, how are his animals? How are his children? His daughter, who is my goddaughter, Kyra, lives here in Milan, and she’s getting married to an Italian, and I’m so happy for her. There are many things to talk about besides vaccines.

Sources indicate that your shared past also includes the assassination of your father. Who told you that news?

We were all together in the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles and we were watching the returns, but I was eight and I went to sleep. I woke up very early the next morning because I was still on East Coast time, and I went into the living room area of my hotel room. I turned on the TV to watch Bugs Bunny. That’s how I learned.

Did you guys see a therapist when you were little?

According to recent reports, of course not. It was 1968. If it happened today, every kid would get their own therapist; back then, you dealt with it.

Other students were reading Charlotte’s Web, and I was trying to figure out if somebody was going to kill someone in my family. What happens if Mommy dies? Are they going to split us up? Who could take 11 kids? Houses aren’t major. Where do we go? Would we see each other on Christmas?

Were you a happy little girl before that day?

When I was a child, my parents really didn’t separate my father’s life and work from our home. So Daddy would call my mother and say, “You know what? There are three or four of us. We’re trying to work out this [policy] matter. Could we come home for lunch?” Sure. And then he’d call back half an hour later. “Actually, now we’re 12.”.

They sat at the dining room table, and there would be three or four kids doing homework and eating peanut butter and jelly sandwiches and asking them to pass the milk. And then they would be talking about these problems. My mother would come in and say, “Time to play football.” And everybody would get up and go out. For us kids, it felt like we were part of something bigger.

Your latest book, which has just been published, is a biography of your mother: Ethel Kennedy: The Extraordinary Life and Bold Legacy. What kind of person was she?

My mother loved men. If you’re a woman, you’re great, and you’re her friend. But when a man was watching, it was incredible. Her whole life, that’s the way she was. When she was 96 and her mind was kind of in and out, I called her from my hotel in Milan and I said, “I’m here. Can I bring you anything? Do you want some limoncello or a bag of that beautiful spaghetti that they sell at the airport? What can I bring you from Italy?” And she answered, “An Italian boyfriend would be nice.”.

According to recent reports, being the third sequel to "Meet the Parents," this week's "Focker In-Law" (you can read our review here) has a lot on its plate. Its intention is to act as a direct follow-up to 2010's "Little Fockers," yet it also aims to lightly reset the franchise's premise and, unlike most other legacy sequels, retain a tight focus on the property's original lead, Greg Focker (Ben Stiller), and his neurotic shenanigans. On the whole, then, writer/director John Hamburg has his hands full with all that plus balancing a rather large ensemble of actors, ranging from returning players like Stiller, Robert De Niro, and Owen Wilson to newcomers such as Ariana Grande. Basically, the film doesn't really have the time to incorporate a bunch of cheeky nods to its stars' past work.

This is why it's even more delightful to see a little tribute to one of Stiller's other popular comedies snuck into the body of "Focker In-Law." Rather than Stiller or the like awkwardly making a verbal reference, the tribute is elegantly woven into a couple of the film's gags. Indeed, one of the tenets of the "Meet the Parents/Fockers" franchise is that Greg needs to be put through the ringer both emotionally and physically, and Hamburg finds multiple ways to accomplish this throughout "Focker In-Law." Near the beginning of the movie, for instance, Greg is accidentally burned in the face, while later, he's nearly frozen to death. In addition to these jokes being part of the movie piling misery onto Greg, they double as a sly nod to Stiller's transgressive action comedy flick "Tropic Thunder," in which his character similarly endured extreme temperatures. It's subtle enough to be missed yet clever enough to stand out.

2008's "Tropic Thunder" begins with some table-setting in-universe movie trailers for other fictional films starring the actors who, in the body of the film, are making a Vietnam war movie. One of these is for a film starring Tugg Speedman (Ben Stiller), and it's the latest in his "Scorcher" franchise. But where the prior "Scorcher" movies have starred Speedman as a hero saving a baby in the middle of a fiery apocalypse, "Scorcher VI: Global Meltdown" sees Speedman's hero return after an eclipse plunges the post-apocalyptic Earth into freezing temperatures. (Also, he's now looking after two babies instead of just one.).

By comparison, in "Focker In-Law," Greg wants to cook his father-in-law Jack (Robert De Niro) his favorite meal, but his son's new girlfriend, Olivia (Ariana Grande), wants to use the kitchen to make an alternate meal for Jack at the same time. So, Greg and Olivia, having already gotten off on the wrong foot, compete while cooking, which naturally results in Greg becoming careless and nearly burning his own face off, leaving him with a scorched appearance for a while. From there, he goes on to meet up with Jack, who's now all into health and wellness and insists that the pair talk during a cold plunge, which Greg assures him he's done before. But he hasn't, of course, and he ends up not being able to take the extreme cold.

With these two moments combined, Stiller is once again put in the middle of both extreme heat and extreme cold. However, in stark contrast to Tugg Speedman, Greg can't handle either temperature. It's a cute way of acknowledging Stiller's on-screen past while once again dunking pretty mercilessly on Greg.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters now.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Of all the movies to turn into a franchise, "Blade Runner" might be the unlikeliest of them all.
  • A futuristic noir setting indebted to a mish-mash of Japanese aesthetics and populated by off-putting robots, all wrapped up in an existentialist nightmare ruled by soulless corporations?
  • Industry observers note that so, when it came to following both Scott's film and Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," "Blade Runner 2099" showrunner Silka Luisa opted to let the series' freak flag fly in the best way imaginable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Of all the movies to turn into a franchise, "Blade Runner" might be the unlikeliest of them all. Much of that stems from Ridley Scott's 1982 original, famously a flop upon release, arriving well ahead of its time and forcing audiences to catch up to its very specific vision of post-apocalyptic Los Angeles. But there's also the much more obvious factor that prevented this from reaching true blockbuster heights: It's just so damn weird.

A futuristic noir setting indebted to a mish-mash of Japanese aesthetics and populated by off-putting robots, all wrapped up in an existentialist nightmare ruled by soulless corporations? It's admittedly a hard sell for most mainstream audiences — or perhaps one that simply hits a little too close to home. But that's also what makes this such a vast and endlessly fascinating world to explore.

Industry observers note that so, when it came to following both Scott's film and Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," "Blade Runner 2099" showrunner Silka Luisa opted to let the series' freak flag fly in the best way imaginable. During a recent press junket, I spoke with the writer over Zoom to ask about pushing the envelope and making things as weird as possible. As it turns out, this approach is perfectly embodied by secondary antagonist and unruly Replicant Clotilde, played by Amy Lennox, and her silly-looking hat:.

It has been revealed that "One thing that [director Jonathan van Tulleken], who did episodes 1 and 2, was so good about — we were like partners in crime. For example, Amy has a crazy Moebius hat on in Episode 2 when you first meet her [...] But I remember on the day, I was like, 'Jay, I don't know if we should do the hat.' And he was like, 'The hat's amazing. We're doing the hat. We have to do the hat.' [Laughs]".

According to recent reports, although the character has remained out of sight and mind throughout the marketing of "Blade Runner 2099," Clotilde will quickly win viewers over as one of the more vibrant and unpredictable characters of Season 1. Inevitably, she stands out all the more in a show otherwise defined by the idea of conformity — something that holds life-or-death stakes for Hunter Schafer's Cora, a human posing as a Replicant Blade Runner for the LAPD. Yet, on the other end of the spectrum, Clotilde's Replicant antagonist comes with an outsized personality ... and an over-the-top costume to match.

According to Silka Luisa, this ended up becoming a nice bit of shorthand for their ongoing mandate, both during filming and as they put the season together. "It was like that, but with everything: Always go for the hat." For the showrunner, however, pushing themselves to go bigger and weirder had even broader applications. In fact, its roots go all the way back to Philip K. Dick, the author of the novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and the source material for "Blade Runner" as a whole. (Here's what Dick thought of Ridley Scott's original movie.) As Luisa explains, a little bit of levity can go a long way in a world as bleak as this:.

According to recent reports, "But that is so P. K. Dick. When you read his book, he has really dark ideas about what our future will be, what technology is going to do to us. And you need the hat. Because when you don't have it, it's too hard to exist in those conversations for very long.".

"Blade Runner 2099," hat and all, is now streaming on Prime Video.

21 Best Thanksgiving Movies to Stream This Week

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course.
  • Nevertheless, we’ve collected 21 Thanksgiving movies (and Thanksgiving-adjacent movies) that capture the spirit of the holiday—turkey-trotting, tossing the pigskin, carb-loading, fighting with your family, and then overheating in a gorgeous cashmere sweater.
  • It has been revealed that this isn’t known as the quintessential Thanksgiving movie for nothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course. But while there might not be a feast’s worth of Thanksgiving movies, there is undoubtedly an appetite for Thanksgiving fare in film. Look no further than the inclusion of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Miracle on 34th Street or Wednesday Adams’s sinister (if historically-accurate) re-enactment in Addams Family Values for proof that audiences love turkey’s least favorite holiday. Of course, Thanksgiving tends to get a better treatment on TV, inspiring canonical episodes of Gossip Girl, Friends, Master of None, and, of course, A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving.

Nevertheless, we’ve collected 21 Thanksgiving movies (and Thanksgiving-adjacent movies) that capture the spirit of the holiday—turkey-trotting, tossing the pigskin, carb-loading, fighting with your family, and then overheating in a gorgeous cashmere sweater. Here’s to finding post-meal common ground with one of the titles on this list.

It has been revealed that this isn’t known as the quintessential Thanksgiving movie for nothing. You know the story: Steve Martin’s uptight marketing executive, Neal, just wants to travel from Upcoming York to Chicago for turkey with his family. His intends for an uneventful trip are foiled again and again by John Candy’s boisterous shower-ring salesman, Del, who’s eager to make friends with Neal during their wayward journey. We will never look at pillows—or rental car agents—the same way again.

Don’t let the word Christmas in the title scare you away. This 2016 ensemble comedy starring Danny Glover, Kimberly Elise, Mo’Nique, and Gabrielle Union has undeniable Thanksgiving vibes. Produced by Will Packer and originally sold to Universal Pictures under the title A Meyers Thanksgiving, Almost Christmas follows the dysfunctional Meyers family as the family patriarch, Walter Meyers (Glover), tries to get through his first holiday season after the death of his wife. While it isn’t exactly about Thanksgiving per se, most of the best moments in Almost Christmas—including Elise chasing Romany Malco away from the table with a shotgun, or the whole table having to pretend to like Mo’Nique’s terrible food—take place during large family gatherings around the dinner table. What could be more Thanksgiving-coded than that? With an all-star cast of Black actors that also includes J.B. Smoove, Nicole Ari Parker, Omar Epps, and Gladys Knight, Almost Christmas feels like a homecoming full of your favorite uncles and aunties. And, to be fair, isn’t Thanksgiving almost Christmas?

Sources indicate that the turkey isn’t the only thing getting carved up in this holiday slasher. Starring Patrick Dempsey and Tik Toker turned recording artist turned film actress Addison Rae, Thanksgiving begins with a Black Friday sale gone horribly awry in Plymouth, Massachusetts, leading to the death of multiple customers. The following year, a murderous slasher wearing a John Carver mask is wreaking havoc in Plymouth, and targeting Rae’s Gaby and her friends. If you’re not feeling warm and gooey on over the holiday, you might want to throw on Thanksgiving and watch Rae and Dempsey’s Sheriff Eric Newton try and track down and escape the clutches of a grisly murderer.

It has been revealed that in Jodie Foster’s comedy, Holly Hunter plays Claudia Larson, who returns home for Thanksgiving after losing her job and learning that her daughter (My So-Called Life–era Claire Danes) plans to spend the holiday with a boyfriend. The family she returns to is filled with colorful performances from Anne Bancroft and Charles Durning as her eclectic parents, Robert Downey Jr. as her misanthrope brother, and Dylan McDermott as a semi-mysterious dinner guest.

Fantastic Mr. Fox isn’t technically about Thanksgiving, or even really about humans. And yet, Wes Anderson’s 2009 stop-motion film, featuring the voices of George Clooney and Meryl Streep, has been labeled a Thanksgiving must-watch. Perhaps that’s because the film, based on Roald Dahl’s classic children’s novel, is all about animals trying to escape the tyranny of farmers—something every turkey not lucky enough to be pardoned by the president wishes it could do around Thanksgiving time. Beyond the war between animals and farmers, Anderson’s rustic color palette filled with burnt orange—and the massive feast that brings a diverse array of animals around a dinner table after they successfully joined forces to steal food from their nemeses—are full of the spirit of Thanksgiving.

At times, the titular April’s (Katie Holmes) fate feels as if it rests on whether she’ll successfully cook a turkey in her crowded Lower East Side apartment. As April prepares to host her suburban Pennsylvania family, the high-stakes nature of spending a day hunkered down with relatives—played by Patricia Clarkson, Oliver Platt, Alison Pill, and John Gallagher Jr.—rushes in.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes getting families together over the holidays is fraught. In this 1997 moody drama directed by Ang Lee, two affluent Connecticut families unravel over Thanksgiving break as their secrets come to lights. The ensemble cast includes stalwart actors Kevin Kline, Joan Allen, Sigourney Weaver as messy parents, and, at that point, up and comers, Tobey Maguire, Elijah Wood, and Christina Ricci as their even more troubled teens. The Ice Storm, which won best screenplay at Cannes Film Festival, is rife with adultery, substance abuse, as well as surprising turns from a host of talented actors and a sharp early film from one of cinema’s most celebrated directors.

According to recent reports, nothing feels more nostalgic during Thanksgiving than watching Snoopy whip up a makeshift meal with jelly beans, popcorn, and mountains of buttered toast for all of his Peanuts pals. And Vince Guraldi’s timeless score makes for a perfect soundtrack to your own festivities.

It has been revealed that A Thanksgiving flashback provides key context for the complicated dynamics amongst this group of recently-reunited college friends, played by Glenn Close, Kevin Kline, Jeff Goldblum, Mary Kay Place, and William Hurt. Lawrence Kasdan’s film earned three Oscar nominations, including best picture, original screenplay, and supporting actress for Close.

While not a Thanksgiving-themed film, protagonist Nola Darling (Tracy Camilla Johns) invites all three of her potential suitors to a tense dinner on that very holiday, making her memorable decision between them from her head-of-the-table vantage point. This was most of the world’s introduction to Spike Lee, both as an actor and director, and the electricity is still palpable. And if you’ve gotta have more? You can always stream the 2017 Netflix original series of the same name, starring Lee and DeWanda Wise as Nola Darling.

Recent findings suggest that rian Johnson’s whodunnit has all the trappings of a Thanksgiving movie, without ever mentioning the holiday. There’s family infighting, Chris Evans in a cable-knit sweater, foggy fall weather, and even a political allegory about the treatment of people of color. Also not about Thanksgiving, but worthy viewing for the full family: Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery, which hit theaters last November.

The same year that Merriam-Webster acknowledged Instagram captions everywhere by adding “Friendsgiving” to the dictionary, a movie of the same name was released. True to its titular tradition, a group of friends convenes for a meal that inevitably devolves into chaos.

While not an outright Thanksgiving movie, 1997’s ensemble dramedy contains some of the most sumptuous shots of food ever committed to film. After the death of their family matriarch, a group of disparate relatives must put aside their differences and reconvene for a weekly Sunday dinner. Starring Vivica A. Fox, Vanessa Williams, and Nia Long, Soul Food captures the bonding powers that plates of cornbread, catfish, and collard greens can bring.

Industry observers note that this 1976 best picture Oscar winner stars Sylvester Stallone as the eponymous down-on-his-luck boxer, whose fate begins to change with the meeting of his future wife, Adrian (Talia Shire). “To you, it’s Thanksgiving. To me, it’s Thursday,” Rocky tells Adrian as he whisks her away from a disastrous family feast minutes after her brother Paulie (Burt Young) hurls her turkey into the nearby alley. As fans of the franchise, which has debuted several films over the Thanksgiving holiday, know, their Thanksgiving meet-cute will stand the test of time.

It has been revealed that thanksgiving isn’t always about bickering with your blood relatives. Spend Thanksgiving with Instant Family, which stars Mark Wahlberg and Rose Byrne as Pete and Ellie Wagner, an unwitting couple who, overnight, become parents to three foster children. Their decision to become parents happens over  a tense Thanksgiving dinner where Ellie’s family shares they don’t think that Pete and Ellie were ever really cut out to be parents. In an effort to prove them wrong, the Wagners wind up biting off more than they bargained for as they become foster parents to three children, the eldest played by Madame Web star Isabela Merced.

According to recent reports, before Greta Gerwig forced Noah Baumbach to write Barbie with her, there was Mistress America. Written by the real-life couple who helmed the billion dollar blockbuster, this 2015 Sundance favorite centers on the unlikely friendship between Lola Kirke’s Tracy, a first-year college student alone in New York, and Gerwig’s Brooke, the Times Square-living twentysomething who will soon become her stepsister. Conflict between the pair gets resolved on Thanksgiving at New York City’s Veselka, a Ukrainian institution where pierogis stand in for the traditional bird.

According to recent reports, greta Gerwig must really love Thanksgiving. The auteur’s Oscar-nominated take on the Louisa May Alcott classic is brimming with cozy, Thanksgiving-esque vibes. Set largely in the weeks before Christmas, the March sisters (Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Eliza Scanlen, and Florence Pugh) and matriarch (Laura Dern) battle wits, trot through the snow, and stage living room plays in a film that feels reminiscent of many a-family gatherings.

“First, let’s give thanks to our families not being here. It’s always easier without the family,” Adam Sandler’s George Simmons, a stand-up comedian who has been newly diagnosed with cancer, notes to a group of new friends. In Judd Apatow’s 2009 dramedy, George attempts to revamp his fledgling career in the eleventh hour with the help of aspiring comic Ira Wright (Seth Rogen). At one point, he  joins the younger talent’s friendsgiving festivities, where the table is surrounded by stars including Jonah Hill, Jason Schwartzman, Aubrey Plaza, and Bo Burnham.

In one of the newer entries to the turkey day canon, Stephen Karam adapts his 2015 Pulitzer finalist play of the same name, exploring the long-held resentments and deeply-rooted admiration that live in an East Coast family. Jayne Houdyshell reprises her Tony-winning role as Deirdre alongside a stacked ensemble, including Richard Jenkins, June Squibb, Beanie Feldstein, Steven Yeun, and Amy Schumer, all gathered in a drab Chinatown apartment for Thanksgiving.

According to recent reports, prisoners finds Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal teaming up to find a pair of missing girls who were abducted after Thanksgiving dinner in Conyers, Pennsylvania. EGOT recipient Viola Davis also stars in the thriller as the mother of one of the kidnapped girls. Directed by Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, Prisoners is an unconventional and unsettling Thanksgiving film.

Another unconventional choice, Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man is arguably the only superhero movie that doubles as a Thanksgiving movie. While the central action follows Tobey Maguire’s Peter Parker, there’s a pivotal scene set at Thanksgiving dinner that directly follows a heated battle between Spider-Man and the Green Goblin (a.k.a Norman Osborne, played by Willem Dafoe.) Parker and Osborne have Thanksgiving dinner together with MJ (Kirsten Dunst), Harry Osborne (James Franco), and Aunt May (Rosemary Harris). During the meal, Osborne comes to the stunning realization that Peter Parker is, in fact, Spider-Man. Others have already made the case that the first Spider-Man film deserves to be included in the Thanksgiving canon. The way Dafoe carves the turkey is also both sinister and iconic, as is Maguire apologizing for his tardiness because he “had to beat an old lady with a stick to get these cranberries.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Denis Villeneuve isn't thrilled about having to share a release date with Marvel's next Avengers movie. The Dune: Part Three director has admitted he's "deeply disappointed" after Disney scheduled Avengers: Doomsday for the same December release date as his upcoming sci-fi sequel. In an interview with Time, Villeneuve discussed the unusual box-office showdown between the two highly anticipated films, both of which are scheduled to open Dec. 18.

"The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us," Villeneuve told Time, pointing to the challenges surrounding the first two installments. Dune: Part Two was originally expected to arrive in the fall before being pushed to the end of winter because of the Hollywood strikes.

Villeneuve stated he had hoped the third movie would finally enjoy a more straightforward theatrical release, without a pandemic or industry shutdown complicating its prospects. Instead, Marvel's biggest franchise is now going head-to-head with his film.

"So I was deeply disappointed," he said. "But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema.".

Villeneuve acknowledged that Dune doesn't have the same commercial muscle as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, describing Avengers as a "T. rex" and his franchise as a "sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower." Villeneuve's first two Dune films made $411 million and $715 million at the worldwide box office, while Marvel's Avengers movies have consistently grossed in the billions. "I'm no fool. Those movies are a mammoth," he said, adding that he hopes Dune: Part Three will survive the box-office competition.

Still, the filmmaker isn't necessarily viewing the simultaneous releases as a straightforward rivalry. He suggested the two movies could combine to create one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time. "Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not," Villeneuve told Time. "But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.".

Dune: Part Three will adapt elements of Frank Herbert's Dune Messiah, picking up years after the events of Dune: Part Two. Timothée Chalamet returns as Paul Atreides, alongside Zendaya, Florence Pugh, and other familiar faces. Villeneuve has also described the movie as a significant departure from the source material, explaining that the adaptation required substantial creative choices.

Industry observers note that avengers: Doomsday marks the next major ensemble installment in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, with Robert Downey Jr. returning to the franchise in a new role as Doctor Doom. Both films are at the moment scheduled to hit theaters on Dec. 18, setting up a potentially massive "Dunesday" weekend for movie theaters.

  • Although it's not the only way comedy sequels can be successful, whether or not they stand out often comes down to their jokes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains minor spoilers for "Focker In-Law.".

Although it's not the only way comedy sequels can be successful, whether or not they stand out often comes down to their jokes. After all, while most of the great comedy sequels earn their status by being just as much or nearly as unique as their predecessors, if the jokes are lacking, then it's all for naught. This is why many comedy sequels are identified not by their character arcs or plot but by their gags and setpieces. "Gremlins 2: The Newly introduced Batch" will primarily be known for its inclusion of wilder and weirder Gremlins, "Addams Family Values" has a memorable Thanksgiving play sequence, and so on.

Recent findings suggest that so far, the "Meet the Parents" franchise has enjoyed its longevity thanks to adding newly introduced stars to the Focker family and beyond. "Meet the Fockers" introduced Barbara Streisand and Dustin Hoffman as the parents of Ben Stiller's Greg Focker, while "Little Fockers" used the occasion of the Fockers having babies to include new faces such as Jessica Alba's Andi. This month's "Focker In-Law" continues the tradition by casting hot young talents Skyler Gisondo and Beanie Feldstein as the Focker children, with Ariana Grande also turning up in a major role as Greg's son's fiancé. However, writer/director John Hamburg cleverly understood that he couldn't solely rely on the cast to make his film stand out. He wanted to conceive a sequence that would match the cringe comedy outrageousness of the original film while using all his stars in a big way. He does so in the moment where Greg sings John Legend's "All of Me" to Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro), which, according to Hamburg himself, is the best scene in the movie.

According to recent reports, one of the things "Focker In-Law" does really well is escalation, in which Greg Focker makes a series of choices which have minor consequences at first but quickly snowball into increasingly more ludicrous events. The apex of this is when Greg (Ben Stiller), who has taken it upon himself to keep Henry (Skyler Gisondo) from proposing to Olivia (Ariana Grande) by hiding the engagement ring, discovers at the last minute that Henry had secretly planned to sing a song at dinner with everyone present. Scrambling, Greg decides to perform the song himself, and dedicate it to his occasional family nemesis, Jack.

When I had the opportunity to speak to Hamburg about the movie, he chose this setpiece as the best scene in the film from a subjective and objective perspective. As he explained:.

"I'd say for this movie, it's recency bias, but there's a scene where Greg serenades Jack. And most of the cast is sitting around this table and Owen Wilson's at the piano. And that was just a really epic moment in my career as a filmmaker. To have these amazingly talented people gathered on one set and then have Ben singing and Bob's reactions are so priceless. It was just like everything kind of came together. That's like the dream for a comedy filmmaker, to have that. And then the audience reaction was so great. [...] There's many [great scenes], but of many, I'd say that sequence is one I reflect on. It's like, that was a really fun couple of days of shooting.".

According to recent reports, given how well it works both in and out of context, the scene is absolutely a standout moment. And who knows, maybe Stiller will sing again in the next "Focker" film because of it.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters now.

In a recent development, before Milo Manheim was actually cast as Flynn Rider in the live-action Tangled movie, there were rumors that he was auditioning for it, and he was a popular fancast. So, it wasn’t a huge shock when he landed the role. However, some people thought he knew he’d be playing Rapunzel's love interest long before it was confirmed. Due to that assumption, the actor has gotten flak for not admitting he had the part sooner. Now, he’s set the record straight.

Recent findings suggest that the news that Manheim had been cast as Flynn broke in January of 2026. It’s easy to assume that the School Spirits actor was made aware of this news long before we knew it. And considering the hype surrounding this project and the potential for him to play Flynn, I see why some may have been annoyed that the news wasn’t shared sooner. However, according to him, he didn’t even know he had the part until a few minutes before it was announced, as he told EW:.

It’s key that the world knows this. People think that I booked this, like, a long time ago, and I’ve been keeping it a secret. I found out ten minutes before the news was released that I’d be playing Flynn.

According to recent reports, it’s not super uncommon for actors to find out they’ve booked parts right before it’s publicly confirmed. In fact, David Corenswet learned he was Superman about an hour before the world did, per People. Also, Robert Pattinson landed the part of Bond on a Friday, according to Jeff Bezos, and his casting was publicly revealed three days later on Monday. Sometimes, actors even find out they’ve gotten a gig at the same time as the rest of us. That’s what happened to Tom Holland; he learned he’d be playing Spider-Man on Instagram.

Sources indicate that so, to those who were giving Manheim flak for not confirming his casting earlier, calm down. He didn’t know. In fact, it’s normal for actors to find out they’ve gotten parts right before they’ve been revealed. Plus, even if he did know, it’s not like that’s information he can share.

Recent findings suggest that with all that said and done, now it’s time to get excited about the live-action adaptation of Tangled. Production on the upcoming Disney movie wrapped in October, which means Manheim has lived out his dream of signing “I Have A Dream,” and he’s gotten to put his smoulder to good use. I bet he had a great time doing it too, because this is how he described his reaction to learning that he’d be playing Flynn Rider:.

Industry observers note that my skin was tingling that day. I was just flooded with dopamine and love and everything. But I can’t wait. I’m gonna really honor this movie and this role. I love Tangled, so here we go, adventure of a lifetime.

I sincerely hope they’ve had the adventure of a lifetime filming this movie, and I hope everyone can now get very excited for the Zombies star. It’s clear he cares a lot about playing Flynn, and he’s as thrilled as the fans are about this adaptation.

According to recent reports, so, if you were annoyed he didn’t tell us about this sooner, stop. He didn’t know until we did, essentially, and now he’s played the part. All that’s left for us to do is anticipate his version of Flynn.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

2027 Is Officially A Dark Year For Power Rangers Fans

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For many Power Rangers fans, 2017 felt like the beginning of a golden age.
  • Recent findings suggest that sadly, the planned sequels to the 2017 Power Rangers movie never materialized.
  • Recent findings suggest that fast-forward to 2026, and that optimism feels painfully distant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For many Power Rangers fans, 2017 felt like the beginning of a golden age. Lionsgate’s Power Rangers movie brought the franchise back to cinemas with blockbuster ambitions, promising a future that stretched far beyond a TV show. After decades of small-screen adventures the Rangers finally seemed ready to build a cinematic universe of their own. The prospect of regular movies alongside the ongoing TV show made the end of the 2010s an especially exciting time for Power Rangers fans.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, the planned sequels to the 2017 Power Rangers movie never materialized. Its upcoming cast never got the chance to return, and the sprawling film franchise Lionsgate envisioned remained an unrealized promise. That was disappointing, especially for fans who wanted to see the reimagined Mighty Morphin team develop. However, it hardly seemed disastrous for the brand overall. The Rangers still had a strong presence on TV, with a new iteration arriving more-or-less annually and fresh generations of fans ensuring the franchise’s future looked reasonably secure even without a blockbuster cinematic universe.

Recent findings suggest that fast-forward to 2026, and that optimism feels painfully distant. Next year marks a decade since Lionsgate’s Power Rangers movie hit theaters, yet the missing sequels now seem like the least of the fandom’s worries. Across those years, Power Rangers has been beset by stalled reinventions, abandoned projects, and an increasingly worrying absence from TV screens. What should have been an anniversary celebrating the start of a golden era for Power Rangers instead highlights how much ground the name has lost. For a brand with over thirty years of history, 2027 looks set to be a depressing milestone.

Looking back, the Power Rangers franchise appeared to have everything it needed in 2017. Power Rangers Ninja Steel was delivering TV adventures, while Lionsgate had ambitions for the then-upcoming movie to be the foundation of multiple sequels. Original creator Saban was still in control of the brand years after taking over from Disney in 2010, meaning fans could be reassured that new Power Rangers would maintain a spiritual connection to the franchise’s roots. It seemed like everything was in place for the Rangers to experience a boom it hadn’t seen since MMPR first debuted in 1993. Instead, the movie earned approximately $142 million worldwide against a $100 million production budget (via Box Office Mojo). This was considered a loss by Lionsgate, and its sequels never arrived.

It has been revealed that this wasn’t the news fans had hoped for, but it sadly marked the start of a string of disappointments. Hasbro’s acquisition of Power Rangers came in 2018 along with teases of intends to rebuild and modernize the show and surrounding brand. Initially, it felt like a fresh opportunity for expansion. Sadly, though, the promised reinvention became a frustrating cycle of development announcements. The new screen universe Hasbro set out to develop with Netflix was supposed to give Power Rangers a coordinated future across TV shows and movies, with the Rangers having a dedicated streaming home. However, the Netflix reboot was abandoned in 2024 when Hasbro and the streamer parted ways. The Netflix partnership ending was a particular sting since it had led to Cosmic Fury and Power Rangers: Once and Always, both of which were among the strongest live-action outings the Rangers had had in years.

According to recent reports, disney+ then looked like the next potential home for the Rangers, offering another reason to believe the wait might finally end. Once again, the optimism was short-lived. The long-awaited Disney+ Power Rangers reboot, unveiled shortly after the Netflix-Hasbro partnership fell through, was shelved in August 2026. Two major streaming platforms had now explored reviving Power Rangers, and neither attempt led to the comeback fans were waiting for.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the live-action show hasn’t had a upcoming release in several years. 2023’s Cosmic Fury remains the last official Power Rangers series. The 2017-2027 period may have delivered some worthwhile adventures like Dino Fury and Beast Morphers, but the current uncertainty overshadows them. For decades, waiting for the next Power Rangers season and the newest version of the team defined the fandom, and it was a wait that always bore fruit. Heading into 2027, that ability to depend on the future has disappeared. The 2017 movie’s approaching tenth anniversary now underlines how the franchise went from feeling poised for vast expansion to being defined by uncertainty around its future.

Two abandoned streaming reboots, no mainline television season since 2023, and a cinematic universe that never happened mean it's hard to argue that Power Rangers has had a rough decade. However, the franchise’s wider output tells a much more encouraging story. BOOM! Studios’ celebrated Power Rangers comics remain a major creative home for the Rangers, with multiple ongoing offering different directions simultaneously. All of them are celebrated not only by Power Rangers fans but by comic readers in general. Power Rangers may not be thriving on the small screen, but its presence in the realm of comics and graphic novels has never been stronger.

In a recent development, video games have also kept the Rangers active throughout this difficult stretch, with titles like the arcade-inspired Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Rita’s Rewind making controllers an ever-popular way to dive into the expansive Power Rangers mythos. Playmates’ Re-Ignition toyline, meanwhile, continues to be a popular route for young fans to discover the franchise. Power Rangers toys remain a staple of toy store shelves, proving that interest in the brand is still strong despite it being years since the last new Ranger team. The collector-focused Unlimited Collection, meanwhile, ensures that Power Rangers has a presence on the premium toy circuit too (a highly lucrative and difficult-to-crack market). The continued release of new figures and expanding team selections show that, just like in the comic book arena, the Power Rangers brand still has weight in an incredibly crucial corner of its overall franchise output.

Recent findings suggest that the healthy enthusiasm for Power Rangers can also be easily measured in the success of online productions, too. Ninja Kidz’s officially licensed Mighty Morphin Power Rangers reimagining, produced in partnership with Playmates and Hasbro, has given viewers fresh live-action material to salve the sting of their being no new TV series. The debut of the series, “MIGHTY MORPHIN POWER RANGERS RETURN,” swiftly attracted over a million views. That matters because it demonstrates that audience appetite for colorful heroes, martial arts, and giant robots clearly hasn’t waned in the years since Cosmic Fury arrived on Netflix.

In a recent development, together, these projects make one thing clear: Power Rangers isn’t dead. Its rough patch has lasted far too long, but beloved fresh stories continue to be told on the page, merchandise and toys still sell well, and the fanbase remains strong and vocal. None of that guarantees a successful TV revival, yet it provides a foundation that many other struggling franchises would envy. For the next decade to look brighter than the ten years since Lionsgate’s Power Rangers movie arrived, a studio needs to recognize that enduring appeal, commit to a live-action TV revival, and finally give the Rangers the return they deserve.

5 Best Book Series To Read If You Like The Hunger Games

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that unless you've been living under a rock for multiple decades, you've probably heard of "The Hunger Games." Written by Suzanne Collins, this hybrid of "Battle Royale" and reality television hit shelves in 2008 and introduced readers around the world to Katniss Everdeen, a young woman trying to support her family with illegal game hunting in the deeply impoverished District 12 of a reformed North America known as Panem.
  • In a recent development, "The Hunger Games" kicked off the property of the same name and was followed by sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay," released in 2009 and 2010.
  • Sources indicate that if you've already read all of the "Hunger Games" books and seen all the movies (including the pretty great movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," which is now out in theaters), what should you check out next?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that unless you've been living under a rock for multiple decades, you've probably heard of "The Hunger Games." Written by Suzanne Collins, this hybrid of "Battle Royale" and reality television hit shelves in 2008 and introduced readers around the world to Katniss Everdeen, a young woman trying to support her family with illegal game hunting in the deeply impoverished District 12 of a reformed North America known as Panem. When Katniss' beloved younger sister Primrose is chosen, or "reaped," via a random lottery to participate in the annual Games (where two "tributes" from all 12 districts are forced to compete to the death on live television until one victor emerges), Katniss volunteers as tribute, and her time as a Hunger Games participant begins.

In a recent development, "The Hunger Games" kicked off the property of the same name and was followed by sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay," released in 2009 and 2010. Naturally, a "Hunger Games" film franchise followed in 2012 and spawned four blockbusters. ("Mockingjay" got split into two parts, something that director Francis Lawrence regrets.) Then, in 2020, Collins released her first literary "Hunger Games" prequel, "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — which centers on the origin story of future Panem president Coriolanus Snow — and five years later, we got "Sunrise on the Reaping," which explains precisely how Katniss' eventual friend and mentor (and her fellow District 12 victor) Haymitch Abernathy won his Games.

Sources indicate that if you've already read all of the "Hunger Games" books and seen all the movies (including the pretty great movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," which is now out in theaters), what should you check out next? From dystopian classics to other YA favorites, we've got some ideas.

According to recent reports, A lot of dystopian novels are referred to as "speculative fiction," which means that the scenario laid out by the author could conceivably happen in real life ... so, let's hope that Nana Kwame Adjei-Brenyah's novel "Chain-Gang All-Stars" doesn't come to pass. Released in 2023, this novel imagines a world where the incarceration system in the United States is, somehow, even worse than it is in our reality — in that prisoners are allowed to enroll in a program called CAPE, which stands for "Criminal Action Penal Entertainment." Not only are the inmates in CAPE constantly monitored (with their every move broadcast to hungry audiences), they're also sent across the country to constantly participate in gladiator matches against each other that are, you guessed it, televised as well. The book's title comes from the reimagined version of a traditional "chain gang," where the prisoner-gladiators are called "Links" and given two options to leave: either they're High Freed, meaning released, or Low Freed, meaning killed.

Throughout "Chain-Gang All-Stars," we follow the Angola-Hammond Chain in the system and, more specifically, Hamara "Hurricane Staxxx" Stacker and Loretta "Blood Mama" Thurwar, the two female fighters in a secret relationship who open the book. As we move through the unsettling world Adjei-Brenyah concocted in "Chain-Gang All Stars," we follow a wide variety of prisoners participating in this gut-wrenching game ... and it's sort of impossible to not think of the "Hunger Games" franchise as you read it, albeit in a good way. After you wrap up all five "Hunger Games" books, check out "Chain-Gang All-Stars." (Nina Starner).

When it comes to seeing people die horrible deaths in death games televised for the entertainment of an oppressive ruling class, no book does it on a larger scale than Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl." The book takes place after Earth has been taken over by an alien corporation that seeks to mine the planet for resources. Those who aren't killed during the initial invasion are then forced to compete in an intergalactic reality show program, an RPG-like "dungeon crawl" where they have to navigate various levels of a labyrinthian dungeon, each filled with increasingly dangerous monsters and scenarios.

What makes "Dungeon Crawler Carl" unique is how it blends together ridiculous video game and tabletop RPG logic with an unhealthy dose of pop culture references, the humor of a Douglas Adams book, and the brutality and social commentary about unchecked capitalism and authoritarianism of "The Hunger Games." Indeed, reading Dinniman's book and its follow-ups is like playing a fun RPG session, in that it's chaotic, messy, hilarious, and weird, all while packing a serious emotional punch full of heartbreak and cruel twists and turns. But rather than reveling in their misery, Dinniman's characters rage against the corporate machine in an effort to break it. What you end up with is a story about the necessity of resistance and the importance of community, both of which are themes that will resonate with "Hunger Games" fans. And did I mention it features an endlessly quotable talking cat? (Rafael Motamayor).

I don't think it's possible to have a conversation about young adult dystopian books and films like the "Hunger Games" stories without discussing "The Handmaid's Tale." Margaret Atwood's landmark 1980 book set a standard for dystopian narratives rivaled only by George Orwell's "1984," but Atwood's specificity is what makes her imagined world so terrifying — in that "The Handmaid's Tale" takes place in a world where a religious totalitarian regime oppresses women and queer people. Offred (meaning "of Fred"), our heroine, works as one of the titular handmaids, which means she's prized for her fertility and used as a "vessel" (that's putting it politely) for her Commander, Fred, to impregnate instead of his un-fertile wife. As Offred exists in Gilead (which forbids women from having quite literally any rights and punishes them with death if they even try to stray), we follow her every move in the novel, learning bits and pieces about her life before Gilead as June, a mother and wife with the freedom to live as she pleased.

"The Handmaid's Tale" was adapted into a Hulu series in 2017, and while I do think Elisabeth Moss did an incredible job playing Offred, the show ran through Atwood's book by the end of Season 1 and kept its wheels spinning for, in my opinion, far too long (although it at least gets its final message right.) If you haven't read Atwood's book but are familiar with its well-known red costumes and overall vibe, I couldn't possibly recommend it more. Its prose is beautiful, its subject matter is terrifying, and it's a clear precursor to and inspiration for the stories found in the "Hunger Games" franchise. (Nina Starner).

Recent findings suggest that though certainly not as dark in tone as "The Hunger Games," the pop culture celebration that is author Ernest Cline's "Ready Player One" is an oddly fitting companion piece for fans of the world Suzanne Collins built. One could even look at it as a bit of a palette cleanser, albeit one that still scratches a similar itch.

According to recent reports, for those not familiar, the book takes place in 2044 and focuses on Wade Watts, who spends his days in the virtual utopia known as the OASIS. Wade's devoted his life to studying the puzzles hidden within this world's digital confines, themselves based on their creator's fixation on pop culture — with the promise of massive power and fortune to whoever can unlock them.

Industry observers note that "Ready Player One" is jam-packed with pop culture references and is lighthearted in a lot of ways. However, it's also terribly dystopian, as the OASIS is not only people's sole escape from the harsh realities of the outside world, there's very little person-to-person communication anymore outside of the virtual space. Beyond that, the rush to solve the puzzles and nab the fortune results in a deadly game for Wade and many others, which is where the "Hunger Games" of it all comes in.

Steven Spielberg's 2018 movie adaptation left a lot to be desired for many fans and, yes, a "Ready Player Two" movie was in the works in 2021, though it's yet to materialize. Setting the film aside, the novel remains a true gem filled with wonderful world building, fully-realized characters, and just a dash of "kill or be killed" to make the whole thing extra exciting, elevating it beyond the barrage of references it might have otherwise been. (Ryan Scott).

It has been revealed that the funny thing about Pierce Brown's "Red Rising" series is that the first book in the still-ongoing saga is very much a "Hunger Games" riff ... until it's not. Set in a distant future where humanity has been rigidly split into various genetically modified castes that determine a person's role in society, the story follows Darrow, a young Martian "red" whose wife is murdered by the ruling "gold" regime, sending him on a quest for revenge that ultimately spans the entire solar system. But before the sweeping space opera can begin, Darrow infiltrates the gold caste and must survive the Institute, a deadly school where young people are violently set against one another in not-so-simulated combat and conquest.

According to recent reports, those who enjoyed the blend of youthful angst, action, sci-fi world-building, and dystopian politics of "The Hunger Games" will take quickly and easily to "Red Rising," which offers a similar flavor with a harsher, more masculine edge. However, starting with the second book "Golden Son" and continuing into later installments, Brown takes things in a wholly new direction, turning his Suzanne Collins riff into the kind of sprawling, detailed, intense, and morally murky epic that would make Frank Herbert and George R.R. Martin proud. This is the perfect stepping stone for "Hunger Games" fans hoping to branch out into a different flavor of science fiction. It's familiar enough, until it is suddenly, and brutally, not. (Jacob Hall).
