📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With 2026 delivering a packed release schedule for Magic: The Gathering exploring classic planes and several Universes Beyond crossovers, Commander players have had plenty of exciting newly introduced legends to build around. From returning to familiar fantasy worlds in sets like Lorwyn Eclipsed and Secrets of Strixhaven to epic crossovers like Marvel Super Heroes, The Hobbit, and Star Trek, the year brought an unprecedented wave of Commanders for casual and competitive tables alike.

According to recent reports, when Polygon spoke with Magic: The Gathering Principal Designer Gavin Verhey about the year's lineup at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, he walked through each major release to highlight what he considers some of 2026’s most powerful Commanders. Rather than focus strictly on raw power ceilings, Verhey pointed toward the legends that spark creative brewing, surprising table politics, and memorable gameplay moments across every 2026 release. Here's a look at this year's 11 best Commanders in the order they were released.

Recent findings suggest that we all love abilities that trigger when something enters the battlefield, don’t we? Well, Maralen, Fae Ascendant takes that to the tenth degree by bridging two of Lorwyn's most recognizable kindred types into a nimble value engine that’s entirely too fun to abuse. Whenever Maralen or another elf or faerie enters under your control, she exiles the top two cards of a target opponent's library, letting you cast one exiled spell each turn for free if its mana value is equal to or less than your Elf and Faerie count.

Verhey noted that "Maralen turned out awesome" and pointed out that "a lot of people have built that one." He has pitched team-up legends for years, and seeing her succeed makes him eager to explore more dual-type pairings like Rin and Seri or Olag and Miau.

According to recent reports, rather than singling out a single hero from the Turtle Power! Commander precon, the standout attraction here is the modular roster built around the “Partner — Character select” mechanic. Inspired by classic arcade beat-'em-ups, the keyword lets you mix and match eligible legends, like Leonardo, the Balance alongside Raphael, the Muscle or Donatello, the Brains, to tailor your Command Zone synergies.

As Verhey explained, "I think the interchangeable Character Select partner mechanic in the Commander deck is pretty awesome there." He added that he loves how these legends "can be interfaced and spliced together," noting that players have gravitated toward the pairings because they combine partner flexibility with punchy abilities. Pairing Leonardo, the Balance with Raphael, the Muscle gives you a prime example, since putting a +1/+1 counter across your board on token entry and doubling damage from creatures with counters lets modest boards turn lethal in a single turn.

Industry observers note that at six generic, one black, and one green mana, Witherbloom, the Balancer carries affinity for creatures and extends that exact same cost reduction to every instant and sorcery spell you cast. Flooding the battlefield with tokens or cheap mana producers turns hefty spells like Army of the Damned and Shamanic Revelation into effortless plays. Once you pair that discount with token doublers like Chatterfang, Squirrel General, even splashy finishers like Exsanguinate or Torment of Hailfire become trivial to fire off for lethal.

Secrets of Strixhaven is loaded with what Verhey described as "banger commanders," and the designer admitted he could easily name around ten standout legends from the set. Even in that crowded lineup, Witherbloom, the Balancer rises to the top as a blast to build around, especially alongside spell-copying payoffs like Professor Onyx and graveyard recursion staples like Eternal Witness.

According to recent reports, this double-faced mythic rare gives Azorius builds strong flexibility at flash speed. On his front face, King T'Challa draws you a card whenever any player draws their second card each turn, and you can pay six mana total to transform him into Black Panther, Hope Enduring. The opposite side of the card yields a double-striking threat with flash that prevents damage dealt to him and draws cards on combat hits, making him especially lethal with equipment staples like Sword of Feast and Famine or unblockable auras like Steel of the Godhead.

Verhey pointed to T'Challa and Black Panther as a standout among cards that fit traditional color expectations while still "tearing up tables." Surrounding him with symmetric draw engines like Howling Mine or wheel effects ensures his front side triggers across every turn cycle before he flips to close out the game.

It has been revealed that at a single white mana, Nick Fury, Agent of S.H.I.E.L.D. looks modest on paper until you read his Power-up ability. Since Power-up reduces its activation cost by his mana cost when he enters that turn, Fury adds two +1/+1 counters to himself while digging seven cards deep to drop a Hero, Equipment, or Vehicle straight onto the battlefield. It’s solid flavor for a 2/1 creature, and has a lot of potential if you know the right way to abuse it.

Verhey described Fury as "really unassuming" yet potent, noting that "Nick Fury, the one-mana white commander, has been really strong." He also shared that he was running all five free spells once Fury hits the board for a single mana.

It has been revealed that the Hobbit brought Middle-earth's more whimsical side to Commander with standout legends like Bilbo Baggins and Thorin Oakenshield, yet Smaug the Magnificent is an absolute beast among them. Built to snowball fast, the 4/3 legendary dragon with flying and haste, and even nets you a treasure token at the start of your upkeep. Worst of all, however, is Smaug’s main ability, which deals damage to any creature equal to the amount of treasures you have whenever he attacks.

Verhey noted that "Smaug Treasure decks look pretty cool" and called him a "really powerful Commander," which is saying something. For just four mana, the creature not only stacks treasures for you every single turn, but also deals a little extra damage where needed, best used to chip away at a player’s life total or creature-filled battlefield. Even worse is that Smaug can swing right when he gets onto the battlefield thanks to haste, so if you already have a slew of treasures by the late game, he’s dealing some serious damage that can be made even more devastating with red staples like Furnace of Rath and Fiery Emancipation.

Just like Smaug, Radagast of Rhosgobel also hails from The Hobbit set, bringing instant-speed tempo to mono-green decks. His static ability discounts the first creature spell you cast each turn by two generic mana and lets you cast it as though it had flash, essentially saving you mana for interaction before deploying threats on an opponent's turn.

The Hobbit offers strong options across the board, according to Verhey, who mentioned, "I like the Radagast decks I've been seeing that discount your spells when you play one a turn." That opens the door for surprise plays like flashing in Kogla, the Titan Ape for instant removal or dropping discounted threats like Ghalta, Stampede Tyrant right before your untap step. While I’m not running him as a commander, I have a Radagast in my Thalia and the Gitrog Monster deck, which is all around sacking creatures and land.

Sources indicate that as a color-shifted twist from the Reality Fracture Commander decks, Dack Fayden, Helping Hand, puts a fun spin on a well-known Magic character. Upon entering, Dack reveals cards from the top of your library until you hit creature cards equal to the number of your opponents. He then puts those creatures onto the battlefield permanently goaded and hands one to each opponent, stirring up chaotic table politics with a hint of group hug thrown in.

Calling the white Dack Fayden "kind of a funky one,” Verhey suggested he might be the answer for raw power in the set. Players who pair his trigger with blink staples like Ephemerate or symmetrical payoffs like Homeward Path and Trove of Temptation can swiftly turn messy handouts into a one-sided advantage.

Liliana the Faultless flips familiar Magic lore in the Echoverse-themed Reality Fracture, becoming a white-aligned version of the character that gains you a life whenever another creature or planeswalker you control enters. You can also pay one mana and discard a card to grant another creature or planeswalker you control hexproof until the end of turn, giving mono-white decks a steady form of protection.

While Verhey also shouted out the set's white Leonin legends and his own black Abzan precon designs, Liliana fits neatly alongside those experiments. Her discard-to-protect clause pairs cleanly with planeswalker or token commanders like Elspeth, Sun's Champion and Mondrak, Glory Dominus that want extra shield equity.

True to his trickster reputation, Q, Stacking the Deck shuffles your library on entry and exiles cards from the top until he hits a nonland card, letting you repeatedly copy that exiled spell by discarding cards from your hand on your turn. Various brewers have already pushed this to remarkable extremes with 98-land decks built to guarantee hitting a specific combo piece.

It has been revealed that verhey admitted he still loves Q and wants "to believe that Q has something pretty wacky," framing him not necessarily as the strongest card in the set, but as one "on my radar" that plenty of players are already building around. Slotting Glaring Fleshraker into a 98-land Q deck, for example, demonstrates just how wild things can get, since exiling lands from your hand to chain copies of Fleshraker floods the board with Eldrazi Spawn tokens that pay for the next copy and ping the entire table out of the game in a single turn.

#167221. Ingrid Bergman and Roberto Rossellini: The Affair That Outraged America

Ingrid Bergman and Roberto Rossellini: The Affair That Outraged America

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The whole situation had become such a mess that their marriage had to take place by proxy, through lawyers thousands of miles away.
  • I saw your films Open City and Paisan, and enjoyed them very much.
  • Recent findings suggest that this now legendary letter above has become part of film history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The whole situation had become such a mess that their marriage had to take place by proxy, through lawyers thousands of miles away. The romance between actor Ingrid Bergman and director Roberto Rossellini was one of the great scandals of the 20th century. They were two married people who had fallen in love and embarked on an adulterous relationship—nothing that hadn’t been seen before, especially in the film industry—but something about their particular situation sparked a wave of international outrage with an intensity that’s rarely seen. There were condemnations from the Vatican, proclamations from the US Senate, insults of every kind, and an avid and destructive interest from the press and the public. There were also some glorious moments, erupting volcanoes, and even plates of spaghetti used as weapons.

I saw your films Open City and Paisan, and enjoyed them very much. If you need a Swedish actress who speaks English very well, who has not forgotten her German, who is not very understandable in French, and who in Italian knows only “ti amo,” I am ready to come and make a film with you.

Recent findings suggest that this now legendary letter above has become part of film history. It’s no surprise that two artistic sensibilities of the caliber of Bergman and Rossellini would connect through the latter’s films—masterpieces of Italian neorealism that Bergman connected with emotionally and intellectually. “The realism and simplicity of Open City were heart-shocking,” she recalls in Ingrid Bergman: My Story. “No one looked like an actor, and no one talked like an actor. There was darkness and shadows, and sometimes you couldn’t even see it. But that’s the way it is in life…. You can’t always see and hear, but you know that something almost beyond understanding is going on.” Bergman left the movie theater where she had just seen the film on a spring night in 1948 deeply moved. She didn’t know it, but her life had just changed forever.

It has been revealed that the world 80 years ago was very different from today, of course, and the actor had a hard time tracking down the director. When she finally did locate him, they began an exchange of letters filled with deep admiration, during which they agreed to collaborate on a screenplay that Rossellini was working on which would eventually become the film Stromboli. The involvement of someone as famous and talented as Bergman should have, in theory, made it easier for Rossellini to raise funds for another film. She was Sweden’s most successful export since Greta Garbo, the Ilsa of Casablanca, and an Oscar winner for her performance in Gaslight. She was admired worldwide for her naturalness and beauty. She was so popular that there was even a reported surge in women choosing to become nuns after the release of another film she starred in, The Bells of St. Mary’s, much to the chagrin of many parents. For his part, Rossellini might not have been well-known in the US, but his revolutionary ability to capture the realities of life on film had earned him a Palme d’Or at Cannes and the admiration of cineasts. He had also starred in various encounters with Italy’s fledgling paparazzi. Married for over a decade, he maintained a relationship that was an open secret, with his lover and muse, the spectacular actor Anna Magnani. Together they were a tumultuous and popular couple—that is, until Bergman appeared on the scene via her letter.

In a recent development, their relationship was long limited to correspondence, but there was clearly some passion in those letters because, upon arriving at the Hotel Luna Convento in Amalfi with Magnani, Rossellini requested that any telegram or letter from England be delivered to him with the utmost discretion. (Bergman was, at the time, shooting Under Capricorn at the Elstree Studios outside London.) The staff assumed this didn’t apply to his well-known partner, and when they were in the hotel dining room, a waiter approached him and mentioned, in full view of Magnani, “I was instructed that if a telegram arrived for you from England, I should give it to you in private. Here you go.” Magnani had already begun to hear rumors about the relationship between Rossellini and the famous Swedish actor, whom he was said to be planning to offer a role that had been written specifically for her. “Now, is this all right—eh, Roberto?” she asked kindly as she served herself more spaghetti with tomato sauce. “Ah, yes, yes, grazie,” he replied distractedly.

Recent findings suggest that “Good. Here, you can have it,” and she tossed the heap of spaghetti straight into Rossellini’s face.

Magnani’s intuitions were right. When Bergman first arrived in Rome to then travel through the south of the country on her way to Stromboli, the island in the Aeolian archipelago where the film was to be shot, she and Rossellini became lovers: “I fell in love with him because he was so unique. I’d never met anyone like him, so free. He brought new dimensions to life, new boundaries, new emotions, and new horizons. And he gave me a courage I’d never known before.” She had been married for over 10 years to Petter Lindström, a doctor who was her first love, but she hadn’t been happy for a long time—neither in her relationship nor in Hollywood. In fact, she’d earlier asked him for a divorce; he refused to grant it, and since they had a young daughter, Pia, and their cohabitation was proceeding smoothly enough, they continued to live together under the same roof. In the eyes of the world, they were still husband and wife. But shortly before meeting Rossellini, Bergman had had a romance with another tormented artistic figure, the photographer Robert Capa. Since that affair had no major consequences, Lindström turned a blind eye. The story with Rossellini would be completely different. He represented a way out of a marriage and an industry in which she felt trapped. “I think I was just waiting for someone to come along and help me out of that marriage because I didn’t have the strength to go. That was over three years before I met Roberto Rossellini.” What she didn’t realize was how much her decision would turn her world upside down.

In a recent development, italy would be a revelation for Bergman. Rossellini introduced her to his circle of friends, including figures such as Federico Fellini, and served as the best possible guide on her journey to Naples, Amalfi, Sorrento, and Messina. In Amalfi, the actress decided that this was more than just a passing fling; it was a love intense enough for her to end her marriage and leave the United States. She wrote to Lindström from the very same Hotel Luna Convento where Magnani and Rossellini had their confrontation, telling him that she had fallen in love and was staying in Italy. He refused to accept the news, and his denial would give rise to much of the drama that was about to unfold.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the new happy couple drove along the country’s roads, which still bore the visible scars of World War II, through one of the most spectacular landscapes on earth. Everywhere the film crew went, crowds cheered them, delighted that the world’s most famous actor had decided to make a movie in their country. At one of the simple hotels where they stayed, Bergman had to leave her room to use a bathroom on a hallway. Fans cheered her on both on her way there and back.

Sources indicate that it soon became clear that their partnership was more than just a creative one. Life magazine photographed them holding hands, and the images went around the world. By the time they arrived on the small island of Stromboli, the shoot, with its many ordinary people recruited to perform in the film, was swamped by press from all over the world eager to capture images of the lovers at the foot of the island’s volcano. The role of a refugee who agrees to a loveless marriage in order to be released from an internment camp and then ends up trapped in an unfamiliar world that is as oppressive as the one she escaped came naturally to Bergman. It reflected her emotional state: She was caught between the joy of being in love, the guilt of leaving her husband, and the doubts and pain regarding her 10-year-old daughter, Pia, who remained in the United States. In Ingrid Bergman: My Story, Bergman recounts, “It was absolute hell. I cried so much that I thought there couldn’t be any tears left. I felt the newspapers were right. I’d abandoned my husband and child. I was an awful woman.”.

Sources indicate that there are images from the shoot in which Bergman is seen in close-up, and behind her are several women in mourning, an oppressive and threatening presence. They evoke exactly what happened to her. The world exploded in anger against its once favorite star. She was portrayed as a lost woman, if not a whore, and an insult to every sense of propriety. Much of the intensity of the reaction was related to Bergman’s previous popularity and her nearly flawless, pristine image. She was seen as an embodiment of a strict Lutheran morality, a sincere and honest woman. (Lindström would later say she was, in fact, a heavy drinker and smoker, promiscuous, and cared only about her career, not her family.) That this almost angelic figure would give up everything to run off with an unattractive, tempestuous Italian director seemed like an unfathomable mistake. Added to this was the intrigue that she was now his newly introduced muse, following the landmark films shot with Magnani. And there was also, of course, Pia’s complicated situation. Rossellini prevented Bergman from returning to the United States, fearful that if she went, she wouldn’t come back to Italy, while Lindström refused to let their daughter travel to Italy. The divorce and custody battle became bitter, filled with mutual accusations and animosity. As a result, mother and daughter went two years without seeing each other. And then, after that, another six. This is how Pia, the main casualty of this love story, would recall those times: “I stayed with him [her father], and my mother left. She was offered a dramatic life, full of excitement, with romantic, wonderful love affairs. It was magnificent for her. But not what came of it. I didn’t experience the splendid side of the situation. In other words, I was left behind. That’s why I see things differently. I was part of what was left behind.”.

As if there weren’t enough elements to this scandal already, it soon emerged that Bergman was pregnant. Senator Edwin C. Johnson referred to her in the Senate as “a powerful influence for evil.” Some of her friends, however, came to her defense. In 1961, she told Lillian Ross of The New Yorker: “When I gave birth to little Roberto, the whole world started to throw stones at me. But I knew I had friends when I received a letter from Ernest Hemingway saying he wanted to be the baby’s godfather. And when I came to New York to accept the New York Film Critics award for Anastasia, Hemingway remarked, ‘I’ll come with you and punch the first one in the nose who notes anything bad to you.’”.

In a recent development, the night Ingrid went into labor coincided with the Italian premiere of Volcano, a film with a plot similar to Stromboli—created by Anna Magnani to compete with her ex’s film and directed by a German émigré to the United States, William Dieterle. Midway through the screening, the press began to leave the theater upon learning that Bergman had gone into labor and been admitted to a clinic. Magnani resigned herself to the situation, knowing that her film could not compete with Bergman’s baby in terms of media interest. Volcano was a critical and commercial failure. And so, in 1950, the boy, whom they named Robertino, was born. The press hounded the hospital relentlessly: One photographer passed off his pregnant wife as a woman in labor by adding padding to her belly; another crawled through a drainpipe to reach the actor’s balcony; others tried to bribe nuns at the hospital with a million lire; and still others, resigned to not being able to get a photo, created montages with Bergman’s and Rossellini’s faces and published them.

The baby’s birth presented a tricky situation. Legally, Lindström could have claimed custody because his divorce from Bergman hadn’t been finalized, which infuriated Rossellini, so they registered the child under Rossellini’s name and that of a “mother whose identity would be revealed later.” Eventually Lindström’s and Bergman’s divorce would be finalized in a Mexican court, where Bergman also decided to get married to Rossellini by proxy. A producer and a lawyer, friends of the couple, stood in for each of them while, on the outskirts of Rome, the real couple stopped into a small church near the Via Appia. “I knelt down and Roberto held my hand and then we went home and told all our friends that now we were married and drank Champagne.”.

The couple settled in an apartment on Viale Bruno Buozzi in Rome and spent their summers in Santa Marinella, a town on the coast about an hour by train from the capital. After years speaking a mix of broken English and French, Bergman managed to learn Italian. The twins, Isotta Ingrid and Isabella, were born in June 1952, and the young family enjoyed a period of intense happiness. But their challenges were not over yet, of course. Bergman’s eldest daughter was becoming a teenager and her relationship with her mother was conducted solely through letters. Living with Rossellini wasn’t easy either. At the height of the tension with Lindström, the director had threatened to kill himself by either shooting himself or crashing one of his sports cars into a tree. Moreover, he was jealous, domineering (he let Bergman work only with him), and at times violent. This was all behavior that Bergman appeared to excuse as simply part of his Italian temper. This is how she describes one episode: “Things were flying through the air, I rush up and I took him in my arms and I started to say…and bang, he threw me against the wall so hard I almost broke in pieces. Well, I mean, I couldn’t do anything. Even to get near him was to risk your life.”.

Recent findings suggest that and then there was the matter of money. Rossellini, who had grown up in affluence, was used to living the high life, but every single movie he made with Bergman was a commercial failure. In 1956, director Jean Renoir approached Bergman to offer her a role in Elena and Her Men. Rossellini admired Renoir so much that he allowed his wife to work on the film, which finally put an end to the frustrating professional slump she had been stuck in for years. After that, she was offered the lead role in a French adaptation of Robert Anderson’s Tea and Sympathy. This is how Bergman recounts what happened: “Tea and Sympathy is the story of a young boarding-school boy who is afraid he is homosexual. Roberto was always disturbed by any sort of homosexuality. When I wanted to send Robertino to a Swiss or English boarding school, he blew up. ‘What!’ he screamed, ‘That’s where it all starts, in those boarding schools.’…The whole theme was too distasteful to him. It wasn’t the writing or the writer; he just hated the general theme. He also hated the fact that in the play I was going to prove to this boy that he wasn’t a homosexual, lead him into sex. The whole part disturbed Roberto immensely.”.

According to recent reports, rossellini tried to forbid his wife from performing in the play, but she ignored him, arguing that she had signed a contract and that she loved the script. He fought back by emphasizing that people would laugh at her and that it would be a flop. On opening night, he snapped at her, “Be prepared when the first intermission comes for half of them to walk out.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not what happened. She was greeted with a thunderous ovation. “The house went wild. You couldn’t stop them. They were standing up and screaming, standing up and applauding, and the ‘bravos’ never stopped. Then I took my solo bow in the center of the stage, and as I bent over, I turned my head and looked at Roberto. Our eyes met. We looked straight at each other. I knew then my marriage was over even though we might stay together.”.

He, for his part, stated: “I separated from Ingrid Bergman because it was impossible for me to continue. We loved each other very much; we had three children…she could return to the industry, but I didn’t feel comfortable in the role of the man whose wife brings home the money. We decided to separate, and that’s why I went to India, as far away from her as possible.” In India, Rossellini began a romance with the wife of his film’s producer, Sonali Dasgupta. Bergman wasn’t outraged when she found out; instead, she calmly proposed a divorce. He insisted on two conditions: that the children never travel to the United States and that Bergman never remarry. She laughed at the absurdity of the requests and refused, saying, “That was just Roberto.” (Shortly thereafter, she began a relationship with the Swedish theater producer Lars Schmidt, whom she married in 1958.).

The custody battle over the Rossellini children was also contentious, almost as much as the one involving Pia. There were mutual accusations of kidnapping and bad faith, and in the end, Bergman ceded custody to Rossellini. The children split their time between Rome and Paris, and Bergman frequently traveled to both cities to be with her children. The couple never completely drifted apart; they remained connected by Isabella’s health issues, including a back operation that nearly left her paraplegic, and the emotional bond that tied them together.

It has been revealed that the world changed very quickly, and the former persona non grata won her second Oscar in 1957 for her role in Anastasia, which was accepted on her behalf by her friend Cary Grant. Bergman heard the news on the radio while taking a bath at her hotel in Paris, where she was staying while performing in Tea and Sympathy. She cried tears of joy in front of her son, Robertino, and soon returned to the United States to resume filming. Her rehabilitation within the industry was complete. She became one of the most respected names in cinema across various countries and languages—a living legend. In 1972, an apology was read into the Congressional Record for the attack against Bergman that had taken place in 1950. At the time she stated, “When I left for Italy, there was a senator in Washington who made a speech against me, and he ended by saying that out of Hollywood’s ashes will grow a better Hollywood.” Bergman didn’t realize her mistake, saying “Hollywood’s ashes” instead of “the ashes of Ingrid Bergman” until she later heard a recording of her comments. She laughed and laughed. “A line I had been waiting 22 years to deliver, and I mess it up!”.

According to recent reports, vengeance was never a part of Anna Magnani’s aims after her separation from Rossellini, beyond that infamous plate of pasta. She continued her career working with Italy’s top directors and even won an Oscar a year before Bergman won her second statuette. When she was diagnosed with cancer, Rossellini sent her flowers despite the years that had passed. She wrote to him asking him to come see her, and from then on they saw each other regularly. Bergman recalls, “When I found out, I called her to tell her I was happy about what she was doing. The circle had closed: She had the man she had loved above all others close to her again.” When Magnani died in 1973, Rossellini agreed to have her buried in his family crypt, and she still rests there alongside him. (He died in 1977.).

Petter Lindström remarried in 1956 to Dr. Agnes Ronavec, with whom he had four more children. He continued his career as a renowned brain surgeon and died in 2000 at the age of 93.

Over time, Bergman would also be reunited with Pia after many years apart. At age 20, following a failed marriage, the young woman—feeling lost and unsure of what to do with her life—moved to Paris to live with her mother and Lars Schmidt. “I came to see Mom in a new light and fell in love with her. Few young women have such an extraordinary, cheerful, fun-loving mother—always ready to go out and do things, see this or that, go to the movies and the theater, dine out, run around, get up early, and go shopping. She had boundless energy. It was amazing.” Shortly after that, the grandmother of her half-siblings—Isotta Ingrid, Isabella (who would go on to become an acclaimed actor), and Robertino—passed away. Pia decided to go to Rome without speaking a word of Italian and take charge of the household, with a cook and a governess, to get to know them as well as find herself. “That way I’d be doing something and mattering to someone. I spent three years with them. Mom sent me money; I paid the salaries and took my siblings to the dentist, horseback riding, and to their lessons. It was a wonderful experience that, in a way, I needed. I didn’t have a specific place in the world; I couldn’t imagine a profession I felt called to; I felt lost. I needed to put down roots, find a place to live, convince myself that I was useful, help someone, and do something that wasn’t just for the sake of doing it.” Rossellini would visit them at lunchtime, talk on the phone about business, movies, and money, and leave after giving everyone a kiss. Pia continued: “I liked Italy. I was happy to be there. I was glad to have met them and to get to know Roberto firsthand, without relying on other people’s opinions or ideas about what he was like; I’m glad to have met Sonali and everyone else, because it helped me observe and understand everything that was happening, to get a sense of how things had come to be.”.

Sources indicate that bergman concludes in her biography: “Someone wrote somewhere about my life with Roberto that I had found a world that for me was probably better than most of us ever attain. And that is true. I did have marvelous happiness with Roberto as well as deep troubles. But trouble is part of one’s life. If you have never had any trouble, if you have never cried, if you have never been really miserable and thought that you could not go on, what kind of understanding would you have for other people who are in trouble?…I think a person who is always happy would be a massive bore. And Roberto was never a bore.”.

"The Hunger Games" franchise is back with a story fans have been waiting a very long time for. "Sunrise on the Reaping" is the darkest movie in "The Hunger Games" series, flashing back to the famed games in which Haymitch Abernathy won. Originally played by Woody Harrelson, that character is a fan-favorite, but this movie does a lot of work to help fill in crucial elements of his character, played this time by Joseph Zada.

Industry observers note that "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place on the "Hunger Games" timeline 24 years before the events of the first movie. It follows sixteen-year-old Haymitch from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes. But Haymitch isn't the only classic character who gets more time to shine in this entry.

Plenty of "Hunger Games" characters return in this prequel in younger form, including Caesar Flickerman (played by Oscar winner Kieran Culkin) and Effie Trinket (played by Emmy nominee Elle Fanning). But they're not the only ones who will be familiar to fans of the series. There's also the matter of Mags Flanagan, a very vital character in the history of both the books and the movies. Originally played by Lynn Cohen in "Catching Fire," she won the 11th Hunger Games and volunteered as tribute during the 75th games.

This time around, the younger version of Cohen is played by actress Lili Taylor. The role is crucial, as Mags is the one who mentors Haymitch en route to his time in the games. But for those who feel Taylor looks familiar, there's a good reason for that: She's a great actress with one heck of a resume.

Lili Taylor got her start as an actress in the late '80s/early '90s, starring in movies such as "Mystic Pizza," "Say Anything," and "Born on the Fourth of July." She worked steadily throughout the '90s in movies, in addition to doing some television, including an episode of "The X-Files." Some of her other notable credits from this period include "Ransom" and "The Haunting.".

It has been revealed that one of her earliest, big breakout roles came in the early 2000s on "Six Feet Under," one of the best HBO reveals of all time, as Lisa Kimmel. She also continued to work very steadily in movies during this period, earning credits in "Brooklyn's Finest" and "Public Enemies," among others. Though not often in the spotlight as a lead, Taylor tends to use her talents in memorable supporting roles.

In a recent development, the 2010s were particularly kind to Taylor. 2013's "The Conjuring" kicked off the biggest non-Marvel cinematic universe, and she had a major part to play as Carolyn Perron, one of the heads of the household at the center of that movie's haunting. It's arguably her most notable role to date. She reprised the role in "The Nun" and "The Conjuring: Last Rites." That same year, she also starred in "Hemlock Grove," one of the first original shows produced by Netflix.

Taylor has over 100 credits to her name so we can't possibly go over all of them, but some other titles viewers might recognize her from include "The Maze Runner: The Scorch Trials," "Leatherface," HBO's "Perry Mason," "Outer Range," "Fear Street: Prom Queen," and most recently Marvel's "Daredevil: Born Again," where she played Marge McCaffrey.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, giancarlo Esposito has spent decades establishing himself as one of television and film's most compelling actors, especially when playing calculating criminals and dangerous villains. Now, the Breaking Bad and Better Call Saul star is taking his interest with the darker side of human nature into an entirely new medium. His upcoming graphic novel, The Venetian, promises an action-packed crime thriller featuring a retired assassin, a kidnapped son, and a brutal journey through Italy's criminal underworld.

In a recent development, with a story centered on revenge, family, and a protagonist forced to confront the violence he once abandoned, The Venetian already sounds like an exciting prospect for fans of the John Wick franchise and Liam Neeson's Taken. However, this isn't simply another story about an aging killer returning to his former profession. Esposito has a personal connection to the project, which explores complicated family relationships alongside its cinematic neo-noir action.

The Venetian is available to pre-order now through this link.

Esposito is making his debut as a graphic novel co-creator with The Venetian, a crime thriller published through Gallery 13, an imprint of Simon & Schuster. At the center of the story is Matteo Moro, a legendary assassin who disappeared from the criminal world 17 years earlier following one final assignment. His decision to disappear wasn't entirely selfish, as he wanted to protect his pregnant partner and their unborn child from the dangerous life surrounding him.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, Matteo's carefully constructed disappearance doesn't last forever. When his teenage son is kidnapped, the former assassin has little choice but to abandon his peaceful existence and return to the world he desperately wanted to escape. There's an especially complicated emotional dimension to his mission because the boy he's trying to rescue has never even met his father. Matteo must fight for someone who doesn't know who he is.

It has been revealed that the graphic novel takes place in Venice, Italy, where Matteo's search brings him face-to-face with criminals and enemies connected to his former life. Its setting offers plenty of opportunities for atmospheric storytelling, with narrow canals, deteriorating palaces, and shadowy corners providing the backdrop for a violent homecoming. Like John Wick, the premise revolves around a highly capable killer whose personal circumstances pull him back into an unforgiving criminal underworld.

Sources indicate that esposito isn't developing The Venetian alone. He is collaborating with screenwriter Matt Wheeler, whose television credits include CBS' reboot of Hawaii Five-0. Wheeler also previously worked with Esposito on the 2024 AMC crime drama Parish, making their reunion on this graphic novel another opportunity to explore crime storytelling together. The project marks Wheeler's debut as a comic book writer.

Sources indicate that artist Jay Martin is responsible for bringing Matteo's dangerous world to life. Martin has experience working in both comics and Hollywood, where his storyboard work has helped him develop a cinematic approach to visual storytelling. His previous comic book credits include Dark Horse titles Behemoth and Lost Boy, the latter of which he also wrote. His involvement makes him an especially interesting choice for a graphic novel built around action and atmosphere.

The finished book will run for 208 pages, giving its creative team room to develop Matteo's history, his complicated relationship with his son, and the criminal forces standing between them. Rather than relying exclusively on elaborate action sequences, the story promises to examine the consequences of inherited violence and the sacrifices parents make to protect their children. The Venetian is presently available for preorder (order here) ahead of its release.

It has been revealed that although Esposito has appeared in several comic book adaptations, including Amazon's The Boys, DC's animated Harley Quinn, and Marvel's Captain America: Brave Upcoming World, creating an original graphic novel is a different milestone. In an interview with People, the actor described The Venetian as a passion project that allowed him to explore his multicultural background while finally realizing a long-held ambition of becoming a comic book character.

Industry observers note that esposito's Italian heritage is especially meaningful to the project. Born to an Italian father and a Black American mother, the actor has drawn on his background while developing a story rooted in Venice. Matteo Moro is also modeled after Esposito, giving the protagonist a visual connection to the actor beyond their shared involvement in the project. That personal investment helps distinguish The Venetian from a typical action graphic novel.

According to recent reports, there may also be a future for Matteo Moro beyond the printed page. According to information from screenwriter Matt Wheeler's agency, Casarotto Ramsay & Associates Limited, a screen adaptation of The Venetian is already in development, with Esposito expected to portray the lead character himself. If the adaptation moves forward, audiences could see the actor take on the role of his own creation, bringing Matteo's dangerous return to life on screen.

The Venetian is scheduled to arrive on June 29, 2027. With Giancarlo Esposito's experience portraying unforgettable criminals, a revenge-driven premise reminiscent of modern action classics, and a creative team with experience in both television and visual storytelling, the graphic novel has the ingredients for a compelling upcoming crime thriller. For readers who enjoy stories about retired killers dragged back into violence, Matteo Moro might be their next favorite antihero.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"South Park" has been on a roll recently. When the show finally left behind its Mr.-Garrison-as-Trump allegory and stopped doing endless specials (even if most of those were fantastic), it found its stride again in Season 28, which took on AI and deepfakes in the funniest way possible. Then, Season 29 took on everything from the data centers, to "looksmaxxing" and "aura farming" in a hilarious "Backrooms" parody, to club sports in a great "Heated Rivalry" parody, to the US beef shortage, and more.

In a recent development, it's been a funny season, and it's been a heartfelt season at times, particularly when the show killed Kenny (again) and decided to replace him with none other than a kid version of Randy (complete with mustache). It has even been a romantic season, with the Tweek and Craig romance-focused episode. What "South Park" usually isn't, however, is scary. That changed with the Season 29 finale, which delivered the scariest TV scene of 2026 — twice.

In the finale, "City Endings," the town of South Park (renamed this season as South America) is hit with major power outages that disrupt the town's "GTA VI" gametime. It is part of a conspiracy involving secret deals the government made with billionaire weenies. At the same time, there's paranoia involving supposed Chinese spies and possible cyberattacks from that country.

In a recent development, in the middle of all this, Cartman, Stan, and Kyle are also haunted by visions of the late Kenny, who died after being blown up by an e-bike in the season's premiere. Except this is not just Kenny, but a zombified version that haunts the boys in the form of horrific ghouls that even infiltrate "GTA VI," like a spectre out of "The Ring.".

In a recent development, "South Park" has toyed with the horror genre before, usually body horror. There was the Michael Jackson parody with Mr. Jefferson slowly rotting away, for example, or the HumanCentipad. The Season 29 finale, however, features one of the wildest and most gruesome eldritch abominations in the nearly 30-year history of the show. It starts with several scenes of Kenny simply standing creepily in the background, stalking the boys as if to try and send a message.

It has been revealed that "City Endings" is a legit horror episode, which is rare from the show that spent nearly a decade on a silly weed farm storyline. The image of Kenny just standing in the background, his face obscured by his hoodie but with bright eyes just shining like Pennywise in "It," is already quite disturbing and terrifying. Then, when the boys finally catch up to Kenny, who leads them to the cemetery and to his own grave, he shows off his gruesome zombie face and starts dissolving like that guy in "Poltergeist," in excruciatingly disturbing detail, before exploding in a pool of blood.

It's enough to make your skin crawl, but it's not even the scariest scene of the episode. That climax comes in later, while the boys are playing "GTA VI" at Butters' house. We see the zombie Kenny monster with long spiky teeth, deranged eyes and elongated limbs with claws crawling out of the TV like Samara Morgan from "The Ring." It is the stuff of pure nightmares, and by far the scariest scene in 2026 television.

The 3 Best Fantasy Movies to Watch on Netflix This Weekend (November 28-29)

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November is a time to be thankful and celebrate with family and friends, and what better way to celebrate than by watching a great movie?
  • It has been revealed that netflix can satisfy all your fantasy needs, too.
  • Let's start with a proper classic, shall we?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November is a time to be thankful and celebrate with family and friends, and what better way to celebrate than by watching a great movie? Once Black Friday is done and all your relevant purchases are done, why not sit back and relax with a great movie set in a distant, fantastical land of magic, danger, and wonder? Indeed, the fantasy genre is a fan favorite, and it has many incredible movies to appeal to any and every cinematic taste.

It has been revealed that netflix can satisfy all your fantasy needs, too. Whether it's a charming tale with hints of adventure and romance or a more sobering take on the genre, the king of the streamers has a strong collection of fantasy movies that are perfect for a quiet evening at home. Worry not, then, and enjoy any of these movies, all of which prove that the fantasy genre is among the best and most reliable in modern cinema.

Let's start with a proper classic, shall we? Conan the Barbarian is based on the iconic character of the same name and stars Arnold Schwarzenegger in the role that made him a star. The film sees a young Conan witnessing the murder of his parents at the hands of the ruthless cult leader Thulsa Doom (James Earl Jones). Growing up to become a strong warrior, Conan goes on a quest to avenge his parents.

Arguably the best sword-and-sorcery movie ever made, Conan the Barbarian is the perfect blend of fantasy, action, and revenge tale. Just as importantly, the film is delightfully camp, the ultimate product of '80s fantasy: bombastic and over-the-top, yet always taking its characters and story seriously. Schwarzenegger was born to play the barbarian, while the late Jones is having the time of his life as the brutally evil and endlessly entertaining Thulsa Doom. Many movies have tried to walk the fine line between absurdity and solemnity that Conan the Barbarian so effortlessly treads, but few have succeeded. Today, it remains an ideal example of how gloriously exciting and enjoyable '80s fantasy is.

Next, we have a more polarizing effort that has slowly earned some much-deserved redemption. Directed by Guy Ritchie and starring Charlie Hunnam, King Arthur: Legend of the Sword tries to modernize the classic Arthurian Legend through — what else? — an origin story. Here, young Arthur (Hunnam) seeks to reclaim his birthright after claiming the sword Excalibur from the stone and using it to fight the tyrannical rule of King Vortigern (Jude Law).

King Arthur: Legend of the Sword is not exactly an all-timer; it suffers from many of the concerns that plague other Ritchie movies, including a case of style over substance and an admittedly anachronistic approach that makes the whole thing puzzlingly distinct. Yet, it's such an entertaining movie, full of energy and gusto, that any flaws are easy to forgive. The action is visceral and well-shot, the production design is exquisite, and the performances are all-around solid. Hunnam makes for a valiant hero, but it's Jude Law who steals the show, playing the sleaziest, most loathsome villain you can imagine. Come for the cast and director, stay for the surprisingly engaging story that will have you hooked from start to finish.

Industry observers note that lastly, we have one of the most delightfully macabre takes on the fantasy genre, courtesy of horror maestro Guillermo del Toro. His version of Carlo Collodi's timeless classic Pinocchio follows the main narrative quite closely, except it sets it in Italy during Mussolini's fascist regime. The plot thus becomes as much a coming-of-age tale as a story of grief, resistance, and what it means to exist in a world where loss is inherent.

Recent findings suggest that guillermo del Toro's Pinocchio is a triumph on pretty much every level. The stunning, stop-motion animation speaks to the director's passion for and commitment to the animated medium — every frame is carefully and beautifully animated, capturing a whimsical yet eerie tone that mirrors Pinocchio's own existence. Charming musical numbers and a powerful anti-fascist statement further make the film a must-watch for everyone who loves cinema. Like other del Toro movies, his take on Pinocchio is somber, melancholy, thought-provoking, and ultimately unforgettable, a treat for the senses and a towering achievement in fantasy filmmaking.

It has been revealed that happy Thanksgiving! There’s a lot of TV to watch this weekend, whether you’re tuning in to reveals that are already airing or looking for your next binge.

The Rings of Power has been releasing latest episodes on Tuesdays, with the finale airing on Nov. 24 (be sure to check out our Sauron explainer). We’re also covering new episodes of Yellowjackets, which air on Fridays (The series premiere revealed one of its biggest mysteries).

When it comes to latest offerings, there’s plenty of exciting stuff. Blade Runner: 2099 premiered this Wednesday, set in a new world where Replicants have replaced humans as the world’s dominant force. If you’re looking for something juicy and bingeable and very awkward for family viewing, The Hunting Wives just premiered its sophomore season, depicting more murders in Texas.

There are plenty of international TV demonstrates this week, including Always on Call and Fool Night, with some anime and reality TV shows newly available to stream. Happy watching!

Set 50 years after Blade Runner: 2049, the series completely shuffles things around. After exploring the dynamics with humans and replicants in two beloved films, the new TV show finds humans as the underclass. The story follows Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human on the run pretending to be a Blade Runner in order to secure a future for herself and her brother.

In a recent development, while Blade Runner 2049 was a direct sequel that continued the story of Harrison Ford’s Rick Deckard, Blade Runner 2099 creator and showrunner Silka Luisa focuses more on exploring the franchise’s themes than advancing its plot. Fifty years after the events of the 2017 film, the Replicants once used as slave labor out in space have led an uprising and now rule Los Angeles. Rather than searching for rogue Replicants, Blade Runners brutally enforce order amongst the humans unlucky enough to be trapped on the barely habitable planet. Desperate human fugitive Cora (Hunter Schafer) is offered a chance at a fresh start if she can impersonate a Replicant to steal something from the police evidence room. When Cora discovers a rogue Blade Runner already took her prize, she has to team up with his former partner Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) to find it.

The Netflix overnight phenomenon The Hunting Wives is back for a second season, building on the first season and novel. This time around, the show is telling an original story, continuing the tale that was first laid out by the book. The fresh season finds Sophie (Brittany Snow) at a turning point: she killed Margo’s (Malin Akerman) brother, leaving her with another secret to hide amid their complicated relationship.​​​​​​​.

If you're into Norwegian dramas,​​​​​​​ Always on Call is now on Netflix. The Norwegian series follows a surgeon who has just started working at an overwhelmed emergency room that serves as a last resort.​​​​​​​ Each episode explores new cases and workplace medical drama that continues to satisfy viewers of all sorts.

Netflix’s newly introduced dystopian anime is set in a world without sunlight, where humanity relies on an optional medical intervention called transfloration. Volunteers are paid handsomely to have a flower implanted in them; it blooms two years later and provides oxygen for others.​​​​​​​ The series follows an impoverished boy who agrees to the procedure, gaining an ability that allows him to hear the voices of Spiriflora. He soon finds himself drawn into a complex conspiracy.

Based on the manga by Kasumi Yasuda and directed by Atsuyuki Yukawa, Fool Night is a surprisingly intimate story set against an enormous environmental catastrophe. Rather than throwing viewers into an expansive science fiction mystery, Yukawa takes his time introducing its main characters and how their lives become intertwined by circumstances neither could have anticipated. It's a more methodical introduction than some might expect, offering plenty of room to establish the people at the center of a world literally steeped in darkness and comforted only by the discarded remains of the volunteers transformed into grotesque flora.

Netflix’s newly introduced three-part documentary series explores the death of police officer John O’Keefe and the case against his girlfriend, Karen Read, who was believed to be the prime suspect. She faced two murder trials.​​​​​​​.

Netflix’s latest reality TV competition follows Salish Matter, a YouTube star who invites seven of her closest friends to a snow-covered getaway for holiday-themed party games. But, since this is 2026 and things can't be that simple, there's an impostor in the group, whose mission is to sabotage all challenges and steal the gifts without anyone else noticing it.

Netflix’s staple holiday cooking series is back with two fresh episodes.​​​​​​​ The Great British Baking Show: Holidays is a spin-off of the beloved cooking show, with previous competitors returning for a season themed around Christmas and New Year’s Day.​​​​​​​.

According to recent reports, blue Exorcist follows a teen raised by an exorcist priest who discovers he's the son of Satan and a human woman. His journey of vengeance against his father begins when Satan tries to claim him as a vessel, with the priest and caretaker sacrificing himself to protect him. The series’ third season is now available on Netflix.

Any shōnen that leverages religious mythology and symbolism to flesh out its world-building is already off to a great start, and Blue Exorcist makes good use of this premise. Two mirror dimensions exist: Assiah, the material world for humans, and Gehenna, the demonic realm ruled by Satan. The demons often breach through the earthly realm via human possession, which is why we have Exorcists, who secretly work for the Vatican and take down these threats. Our protagonist is Rin Okamura (and to an extent, his twin Yukio), who learn that they’re sons of Satan after witnessing their human father’s death.

Avengers: Doomsday TV Spot Confirms RDJ's Doctor Doom Has A Scarred Face

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Marvel Comics fans know Doctor Victor von Doom is scarcely ever seen without his iron mask — a mask that hides his supposedly horribly scarred face.
  • Now, Chris Evans has claimed that Doom wears his mask for the entirety of "Doomsday." But that could only mean he'll keep the mask on until "Secret Wars." Even then, there's the chance that Doom is so disfigured that his face isn't even recognizable as RDJ.
  • In this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marvel Comics fans know Doctor Victor von Doom is scarcely ever seen without his iron mask — a mask that hides his supposedly horribly scarred face. But with Marvel Studios choosing former Tony Stark actor Robert Downey Jr. to play Doom in the upcoming "Avengers" movies "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars," there's been an expectation that Doom's mask coming off will be a jaw dropping moment.

Now, Chris Evans has claimed that Doom wears his mask for the entirety of "Doomsday." But that could only mean he'll keep the mask on until "Secret Wars." Even then, there's the chance that Doom is so disfigured that his face isn't even recognizable as RDJ. A latest TV spot for "Doomsday" does suggest Doom has his scarred face, while also teasing we're eventually going to see exactly what's under his mask ... but not yet.

In this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all. But Doom does not restrict himself to the laws of science. There's evidently a magical seal on the mask (note there appear to be runic designs across Doom's costume), because glowing green tendrils extend out from Doom's hood and grab the mask, slamming it back onto Doom's face. A brief glimpse of Doom's face, visible through the mask's eyeholes, demonstrates hints of pale macerated skin and scar tissue.

Industry observers note that in the "Fantastic Four" comics, it was originally remarked that Doom suffered his scars during an experiment in college. A machine he built to contact the "nether world" (later revealed to be an attempt to reach his mother's damned soul) exploded in his face, leaving him scarred.

Recent findings suggest that now, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby intended that Doom actually only had a thin facial scar — but Doom's ego can't stand even that small imperfection. Later "Fantastic Four" writer/artist John Byrne melded the two ideas. The machine explosion only slightly damaged Doom's face, but then Victor — convinced his face was already ruined — put his freshly forged mask on before it cooled, and that is why he has a horribly scarred face.

The greatest source of Doom's torment is completely self-inflicted. The exemplary 1989 "Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment" goes with Byrne's interpretation. When Doom seeks out the wisdom of the wizard named the Aged Genghis, the sorcerer alludes to Doom's "minor disfigurement." We then see Doom's (barely scarred) face as Victor lashes out at the insult.

It has been revealed that it's unclear what origin "Doomsday" will go with, if any of them. Marketing suggests the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Doom will be driven by a lost wife and child, not his mother. What is clear from this TV spot is that Marvel fans can expect to see Doom and Magneto — the two greatest villains of Marvel Comics — clash onscreen. Doom's wizardry here refutes the obvious conclusion that Magneto wins easily because he controls metal and Doom is concealed inside metal armor.

"He is pain, he is extinction," Magneto declares, setting up Doom's famous third person double entendre: "I am Doom!" Ian McKellen's Magneto was the first villain of the Marvel movie boom that kicked off with 2000's "X-Men." Bringing him back to face (and presumably fall to) Doom is some classic carnival barker marketing that would make Stan Lee proud.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is set for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that supernatural may have ended over six years ago, but the series is still a fan-favorite when it comes to rewatches with your Peacock subscription. The show’s 15 seasons were a roller coaster ride involving the Winchester brothers fighting just about everything Hell would throw at them, and more. However, Supernatural’s controversial series finale has given fans a lot to talk about, and a lot of it is not great. After hearing Jensen Ackles’ own version of the ending, I wish we had gotten that instead.

Sources indicate that the Supernatural series finale in November 2020 saw Ackles’ Dean getting killed while on a hunt and Sam (Jared Padalecki) living the rest of his life with an unknown wife and a son who was named after his brother. Sam eventually died of old age and met back up with Dean in Heaven. It’s been previously revealed the SPN finale was very different pre-COVID, and a lot of it changed and people had to be cut out, understandably.

Ackles reiterated what the ending would have been had it not been for COVID while at a Supernatural fan convention ( via tvdkami), and I am once again mourning what the pandemic took from us:.

Recent findings suggest that loved to have actually gotten to shoot the ending that we were intending to shoot. That being said, that doesn’t change the outcome of how it ended. So if we got to do the ending that was originally scripted, which I think a lot of you know, and for those that don’t, was Sam comes to Heaven and walks up to The Roadhouse, and I come out, and we have that little meeting that we ended up having on the bridge.

I would have loved more than anything for this to actually happen. The amount of characters that Supernatural introduced and killed off during its run, or just straight-up forgot about, was a large number. He went on to talk about Kansas performing, a moment that would have been absolutely perfect, given that “Carry On Wayward Son” was SPN’s unofficial theme song. It would have looked like this:.

According to recent reports, but then I say, ‘Hey, come in here. Some people I want you to see.’ We walk through The Roadhouse, it’s all the people from the show, all the characters. The actual band Kansas was going to be the ‘Roadhouse band.’ And then they were signed on to do it. I think one of them was on a plane about to head to Vancouver when they got the call and said, ‘Hey, we’re shutting down. Get off the plane.’.

Of course, there is only so much that could have been done at the time with all the restrictions, and at the very least, the series brought back Jim Beaver as Sam and Dean’s late surrogate father, Bobby Singer. That was better than nothing, in my opinion.

There were a lot of expectations for Supernatural's finale, and it's still disappointing to think about, even considering the extenuating circumstances. That hasn't stopped Ackles from sharing his own take about what he would have done with the finale.

For him, he also feels like there was a missed opportunity to end the show on a twist, something Supernatural was known for doing.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Sources indicate that so I would have liked for that to happen, but I’ll add just a little extra to that, which is during that kind of reunion, so to speak, I would have liked Jack to come through the front door and just walk up to Sam and Dean and be like, ‘I need to send you guys back.’ And then that’s the end. Then we’re just like, ‘What? Well, wait!’ Which just would have been great, which just opens the door right to something into the future. We can still do it. Not too late. But, by the way, we could go back to that bridge and be just looking out and pull back, and Jack’s behind us, and he’s like, ‘Guys, I hate to do this to you.’.

Sources indicate that I would have been alright with an ending like this, despite it's shocking nature. Though I'll admit it's mostly because I wasn’t fond of how the finale turned out. Dean’s death dragged on, the penultimate felt more like a finale with how Sam, Dean and Jack defeated God/Chuck, and Castiel dying. Yes, things could and should have been different and they worked with what they had, but I still wish it had played out in a different manner.

In a recent development, having recently rewatched Supernatural, I saw the finale again, and definitely think it could have been better. However, I’m just glad the series was able to still knock out a finale given the circumstances, and we can still extrapolate out all of this stuff from the cast in hindsight. Could have, should have, would have.

Prime Video has been serving up a feast for romantic comedy fans in 2026. Lili Reinhart's rom-com "The Love Hypothesis" just finished dominating the Prime Video charts, which came in the wake of Ester Expósito's romantic thriller "Drawn Together" becoming a Prime streaming hit. Now, the streamer has added a Christmas-themed romance just in time for the holidays, and this one stars "Landman" actor Michelle Randolph.

Recent findings suggest that the film is called "Clashing Through the Snow" and before you immediately close this window just let me explain. Yes, the name sounds like the result of a "give me a cheesy Christmas rom-com title" ChatGPT prompt, but Randolph alone should pique your interest. The actor has quietly been delivering standout performances in Taylor Sheridan's "Landman" and his "Yellowstone" prequel "1923." The former sees her play Ainsley Norris, the ditzy but determined daughter of Billy Bob Thornton's oil man Tommy Norris. Based on her performances in those highlights, Randolph surely has a bright future ahead. While "Clashing Through the Snow" might not be her major breakthrough, it's doing pretty darn well on Prime Video.

In a recent development, until recently, Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale's sports movie "Madden" was topping the Prime Video charts. But it's now been knocked out of the top spot by this festive romance movie, in which publishing editor Hannah Hendricks (Randolph) is forced to take a road trip with her rival, Ryan Mitchell (Chris Briney). You can see where this is going.

Sources indicate that according to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, the film has now hit number two on the United States overall Prime Video chart (which combines TV and films) as of Thanksgiving day, and sits at number one on the movie chart. But Michelle Randolph's comedy is proving popular elsewhere, too. In fact, it's become a global hit. At the time of writing, the film is charting on 61 countries' top 10 movie rankings, which is a pretty good showing. Even more impressive, "Clashing Through the Snow" is number one on the movie charts in 47 of those countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Meanwhile, the movie has managed to break into the overall chart in 30 countries, taking the top spot in five of them. That means "Clashing Through the Snow" is the most-watched piece of media on Prime Video in Austria, Poland, Portugal, South Africa, and Switzerland. It even managed to hit number one on the overall chart in the U.S. on November 25, 2026. That's a notable achievement, as often films will break into the top 10 movies without making it onto the overall charts. "Clashing Through the Snow" must be good, then...

"Clashing Through the Snow" is a comfortingly familiar rom-com outing that's perfect for the holidays. The film sees Chris Briney's Ryan Mitchell and Michelle Randolph's Hannah Hendricks stranded at an airport during a snowstorm, after which they share a rental car and set out on a cross-country trip to Latest York. The pair both need to close a deal in order to save their jobs — but wouldn't you know it, they fall in love instead. Along the way there's plenty of romantic Christmas movie moments as the couple stop in charming small towns and overcome mishaps together. Is "Clashing Through the Snow" pushing the boundaries of rom-coms? No. Is it charming? Sure is.

The film is directed by Carlson Young, who made her feature directorial debut with the 2021 fantasy horror "The Blazing World" before directing Sophie Turner in 2025's "Trust." She also oversaw a couple of Prime Video rom-coms before "Clashing Through the Snow," directing 2024's "Upgraded" and 2026's "The Last Sunrise.".

Now, she's delivered a major hit with her Randolph-led Christmas rom-com, which has a 77% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. There aren't enough reviews to earn it a critic score yet, but while William Bibbiani of TheWrap found it to be "unapologetically clichéd" he also found the dialogue to be memorable and saw the film as "an efficient delivery mechanism for semi-believable rom and semi-funny com.".

If that sounds appealing, "Clashing Through the Snow" is streaming on Prime Video right now.

The holiday movies have officially taken over the 2026 TV schedule, and I could not be happier. Between Hallmark’s Countdown to Christmas lineup, Netflix’s releases, and even Hulu’s 12 Dates of Christmas, the options have been endless. Now, Prime Video is getting in on the fun with the release of Clashing Through the Snow. As of writing this, the festive flick is sitting in the number three spot on the streamer’s trending charts, but don’t let the popularity fool you. Some fans are really upset that the film featured a character asking ChatGPT for relationship advice, and I agree with their outrage.

Recent findings suggest that the romantic comedy follows rival book editors Hannah (Michelle Randolph) and Ryan (Christopher Briney) who, after learning their jobs were in jeopardy unless they could wow their boss, set out to land major book deals. When weather and a series of misfortunes halt their respective travel aims, the two begrudgingly agree to road trip to New York together. The proximity allows them to bond, and sparks start to fly, complicating their career ambitions.

Clashing Through the Snow is overflowing with witty banter, memorable scenes, and hilarious and endearing side characters, which is why it was so upsetting when Ryan opted to ask ChatGPT for relationship advice instead of calling his friend Walter (Andrew Schulz), who had already given him advice earlier in the film.

Fans were not happy with the unexpected turn and promptly turned to Twitter to air their grievances over the egregious use of AI:.

Things weren’t much better over on Threads, where fans also made their distaste for the inclusion abundantly clear:.

I don’t know what’s more upsetting: the fact that the film had a Ryan ask ChatGPT for advice or the fact that he was a senior book editor with human friends he could have turned to.

What might be the most infuriating thing is that apparently there was a version of Clashing through the Snow where Ryan did turn to a human instead of ChatGPT. At least that’s what Carlson Young, the film’s director, told Deadline before defending her decision to go with the scene in the film, saying:.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

I personally thought that him talking to Chat was so Ryan. It made me laugh so much. And the amount of times that I’ve caught my husband… I’m like, ‘Are you asking ChatGPT a question? Like for real? Are you serious? ‘And he is serious. It just felt really modern and so of the times, and something like his character would actually do. And I like a lot the responses that Chat has for him. It just made me laugh.

Maybe I missed something, but I can’t wrap my head around hopeless romantic, pragmatic Ryan being the character who would turn to ChatGPT to ask for serious relationship help. That seems like a job he would have wanted a human who can experience actual love to help with, like Walter or even some random stranger he could have stumbled upon.

It has been revealed that as upsetting as it is to see an amazing character turn to AI for help, I don’t think one scene should tarnish the rest of the movie. Clashing Through the Snow is a swoonworthy and hilarious rom-com that does deserve its flowers. Dare I say it might be Briney's best rom-com role (yes, even better than his portrayal as Conrad Fisher in The Summer I Turned Pretty).

Clashing Through the Snow is streaming now for those with an active Prime Video subscription.

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a significant discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

According to recent reports, xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink swiftly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

In a recent development, the X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

According to recent reports, these upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also notable to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

John Hughes made some of the most beloved movies of all time in his eight directorial efforts, to the point where it's nearly impossible to rank the films he wrote and directed. Still, there are few movies that reach the specific balance of comedy with such an emotional punch as Hughes does in 1987's "Planes, Trains and Automobiles." This is a goofball movie that borders on the surreal, with some of the most bizarre imagery in a comedy movie, while also delivering some of the most heartbreaking and heartwarming moments that came out of the 1980s.

Recent findings suggest that the film stars Steve Martin as Neal Page, an uptight marketing executive forced to be paired with Del Griffith (John Candy), a goofball salesman with a heart of gold, when their journey from Newly introduced York City to Chicago is disrupted. What was meant to be just a short cab and plane ride home just in time for Thanksgiving ends up being a three-day odyssey full of shenanigans, attempted murder, and much more.

It's no wonder, then, that "Planes, Trains and Automobiles" is the No. 1 movie streaming on Paramount+ on Thanksgiving Day 2026. After all, there are plenty of movies about Christmas, to the point where it's easy to overlook Thanksgiving, and with good reason. For one, it's not really a holiday outside the U.S. and Canada (and even then, celebrated on different days), and the imagery is not dissimilar to Christmas anyway. Still, the best Thanksgiving movies deliver a very specific tone that's less about holiday magic and more about celebrating what we have despite the horrors of daily life. From the opening minutes of "Planes, Trains and Automobiles," it's clear this movie could not be set at any other time of year except during the chaos and anxiety of Thanksgiving.

In a recent development, the travel chaos that is quite unique to Thanksgiving is the crux of "Planes, Trains and Automobiles." The arrival of snowstorms that plague the East Coast of the continental United States, the huge flux of travelers, and the general anxiety and irritability of travelers around the country add to, well, a very stressful time of year. It's why Steve Martin's uptight businessman Neal is so relatable. The film simply nails the feeling of needing to interact with others and ask for their help while being utterly frustrated with having to deal with anyone at such a bad time. It's also why John Candy's performance is such a tightrope, because his character has to be annoying in addition to being charming. Del's not really someone you'd want as a travel companion, yet he is absolutely the best person you want as a friend.

That tricky balance is what makes the movie so memorable, and why John Candy's best line remains the best Thanksgiving movie quote ever. Neal and Del are forced to not only set aside their differences, but actually recognize the humanity in each other while acknowledging that they themselves are flawed. This is a highly empathetic film that's all about how we should find love and camaraderie even in unlikely companions. That is why the film so perfectly captures the spirit of Thanksgiving, because it's not about estranged family members, but rather complete strangers who must come to learn they need one another and that they should be grateful for what they bring into each other's lives. Togetherness is not just for family members, or even people you like, but also for strangers you come to appreciate despite the ways they annoy you.
