According to recent reports, but for all his prowess, Thornton couldn't shine without a stellar supporting cast that elevates the drama. Ali Larter co-stars as Tommy's fiery ex-wife, Angela, injecting chaotic energy and dark humor into his fractured personal life. Demi Moore (Cami) and Jon Hamm (Monty) command the screen as M-Tex Oil’s powerful elite, while Jacob Lofland (Cooper) and Michelle Randolph (Ainsley) bring the perspective of the younger generation as Tommy's children. Together, this ensemble transforms a high-stakes and dangerous story into one about humanity's pursuit of ambition, survival, and family. However, this show's cast, especially mature actors like Thornton, Larter, and Moore, have played different characters in their extensive careers, and for Larter, one of her most memorable roles is in the cult favorite horror franchise, Final Destination.

Larter portrayed Clear Rivers in the first two installments, anchoring the franchise's early supernatural dread with fierce resilience and sharp survival instincts. It is a stark contrast to her manipulative, larger-than-life turn as Angela in Landman, showcasing her impressive dramatic range. Final Destination has been an enduring franchise that has defied death, and last year, it returned for a very successful sixth installment. Before that, Newly introduced Line and Warner Bros licensed past movies to streaming services like HBO Max. Unfortunately, the licensing agreement expires this month, and the movies will be removed from the service in 3 days.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

Recent findings suggest that you carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the potential plot for Elden Ring 2 has left gamers split due to the original Elden Ring’s multiple endings.
  • The other endings can drastically impact what it would mean for the future of the Lands Between, and this has become a serious topic of discussion among fans who are thinking about a potential sequel to the legendary RPG by FromSoftware.
  • That thread, however, invoked tons of opinions from fans, who argued in favor of or against some of the best and worst endings in Elden Ring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the potential plot for Elden Ring 2 has left gamers split due to the original Elden Ring’s multiple endings. Depending on the choices you make during the game and the questlines you follow during the campaign, you may unlock different endings for the game. In total, there are six different endings for Elden Ring, each of which focuses on a certain aspect of lore. The regular one, for example, is centered around the Tarnished becoming an Elden Lord, even though the fate of the Lands Between isn’t really changed by that.

The other endings can drastically impact what it would mean for the future of the Lands Between, and this has become a serious topic of discussion among fans who are thinking about a potential sequel to the legendary RPG by FromSoftware. User backwards_watch on Reddit initiated a conversation thread showcasing Melina in the Frenzied Flame ending, talking about how they want to play Elden Ring 2 to “know how she’s going to kill me.” This is because this is the only ending in which Melina can be saved, but at the cost of burning the Lands Between in eternal flames.

That thread, however, invoked tons of opinions from fans, who argued in favor of or against some of the best and worst endings in Elden Ring. User marry_me_jane, for example, mentions that the fact that if the Lord of the Frenzied Flame ending is considered canon, then there is no possibility for a sequel, since everything will have been destroyed. In response to that argument, user Distinct-Office-609 mentions that FromSoftware is going to make the sequel set a thousand years after the original game, mentioning that “time is convoluted.” This wouldn’t be completely surprising.

FromSoftware has done something similar with Dark Souls and its sequels in the past, where sequels’ plots take place millennia after the previous iterations. If the official release of Elden Ring 2 does ever happen, it could be that it never acknowledges a canon ending for the original, simply taking place in crossover locations in the Lands Between, eons after the Elden Lords and gods of the original have fallen for any number of reasons. User Tofu_Gundam mentions that “Miyazaki will never ever give you anything resembling closure,” and that lines up with the idea of a partially disconnected sequel.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, there is something enticing about a sequel where the Frenzied Flame ending is considered canon. It’s the only one in which Melina survives. While it is described as the end of everything because the Frenzied Flame consumes everyone and everything, like Midra in Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree, life can persevere in other species, like Farum Azula and the Shadow Realm, as mentioned by user Cw3538cw. In such a scenario, Melina could, indeed, exact her revenge by choosing a new Tarnished to overthrow the Lord of the Frenzied Flame from that specific Elden Ring ending.

It has been revealed that overall, the conclusion is that there are many different possibilities for a sequel. It’s unlikely that FromSoftware will acknowledge one single ending to the game as canon, and as a soulslike fan, the best guess is that the developers would make the sequel set thousands of years after the events of the original. For now, however, there is no official talk about a true sequel to Elden Ring, as FromSoftware is working on The Duskbloods, which has been delayed to 2027.

It has been revealed that there are classic Christmas movies like "It's a Wonderful Life" and "National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation," and then there are the Christmas movies that we just watch every year because they're on repeatedly, forcing their way into the holiday zeitgeist, regardless of quality. "Jingle All the Way" is one of those movies.

According to recent reports, remembered as a comedy that glorifies the hollow commercialism of the holiday season, "Jingle All the Way" was far from a critical darling. But Roger Ebert at least had some praise for it back in 1996, writing:.

"I liked a lot of the movie, which is genial and has a lot of energy, but I was sort of depressed by its relentlessly materialistic view of Christmas, and by the choice to go with action and (mild) violence over dialogue and plot. Audiences will like it, I am sure, but I have to raise my hand in reluctant dissent and ask, please, sir, may we have some more goodwill among men? Even TurboMen?".

Honestly, we should probably be throwing more praise at "Jingle All the Way." While it might depict the unfortunate side of holiday shopping greed and consumerism, it's hard to deny how much fun it is to watch Arnold Schwarzenegger scramble to find a Turbo Man action figure, while Sinbad taunts and thwarts him at every turn. It's a cinematic masterpiece compared to "Jingle All the Way 2" with Larry the Cable Guy, proving it's a Christmas movie that didn't need a sequel.

According to recent reports, but one of the best parts of "Jingle All the Way" comes from the interaction that Schwarzenegger's Howard Langston has with his deceptively thoughtful, sleazy neighbor Ted (the late, great star of "Saturday Night Live" and "The Simpsons," the one and only Phil Hartman). That's where we get one of the best Christmas movie quotes of all time.

Here are some more memorable quotes from "Jingle All the Way," though they might not be as versatile as our favorite:.

It has been revealed that "I'm not a pervert! I just was looking for a Turbo Man doll!" – Howard Langston.

"How about these stupid letters from kids to Santa at the North Pole: 'Dear Santa, can you send me a bike and a slinky?' No! Your father's been laid off!" – Myron Larabee.

"I'm gonna deck your halls, bub." — Huge Santa.

Industry observers note that "They sit there and use subliminal messages to suck your children's minds out! And I know what I'm talking about because I went to junior college for a semester and I studied psychology so I'm right in there, I know what's going on. And then they sit there and they make your children feel like garbage and you, the father, who's working 24/7 delivering mail so you can make an alimony payment to a woman that slept with everybody at the post office, but me! And then when you get the toy, it breaks and you can't fix it because it's little cheap plastic!" – Myron Larabee.

"That really was a bomb? This is a sick world we live in! Sick people!" – Myron Larabee.

Sources indicate that "You know what? Nobody likes you, Booster." – Myron Larabee.

"It's Turbo Time!" – Howard Langston as Turbo Man.

"Ta-ta, Turtle Man!" – Myron Larabee as Dementor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that netflix has completely changed the game in terms of the future of television, as the format of binge-watching has now become the standard for which all streaming services release their content. Although HBO was the network that kicked off the era of “prestige television” through its high-quality writing and acting, Netflix is responsible for getting bigger stars, bigger budgets, and more eyeballs on its programming.

It has been revealed that netflix has never been consistent in terms of its output, as there is no way to guess which of its reveals will end up breaking out to become a phenomenon, but one of the joys of its release strategy is that it can often bring obscure shows into the spotlight and introduce them to a much broader audience than would have ever independently checked them out based purely on word-of-mouth buzz. The standout titles have truly become pop culture events, making them essential Netflix series to watch before kicking the bucket.

Stranger Things is not only the most culturally relevant and massive show in Netflix’s history in terms of what it did to expand a brand, but also a highly influential achievement that ushered in a fresh wave of nostalgia for the classic films of the 1980s. While it has been debated whether Stranger Things became too reliant on its own worldbuilding and foreshadowing for its own good, it is hard to deny how exciting it was when it came out of nowhere to be a hit.

Stranger Things will likely be better remembered for its characters than its plot, as the best that can be said about the more divisive final two seasons of the show is that it continued to provide a platform to a cast of young stars who truly grew into their roles as the series progressed and got more mature.

BoJack Horseman is unlike anything that has ever been done before in terms of animation, as it is simultaneously a deeply rich satire of Hollywood, a hilarious adult animated sitcom that offers an endless array of puns, and an existential, harrowing character study about the nature of addiction, loss, sexual exploration, and trauma. That BoJack Horseman is so consistently charming in its quirky approach to worldbuilding was necessary in order to keep its audience engaged, as the series goes to some very dark places that would have otherwise been challenging to reckon with.

BoJack Horseman looked at the messiness of existence in a profound way that demonstrated a remarkable lack of judgment for its characters, and the fact that it was able to air for six seasons and amass a significant following in the process is a minor miracle when considering the subject material.

The Crown is a highly ambitious series that took on the challenging task of exploring the entire history of the modern British Royal Family through the eyes of Queen Elizabeth II, who ascended to the throne after the death of her father, King George VI. Elizabeth’s rule of over 70 years obviously gave the showrunners a ton of material to draw from, especially when considering that she was alive for almost the entirety of its run.

According to recent reports, the Crown was able to smartly encompass the enormity of contemporary British history by essentially diving itself into three two-season arcs, each of which swapped out the main cast in order to appropriately fit the age of the characters. The Crown is a highly informative (if not entirely accurate) look at history that offers a comprehensive perspective on the evolution of the monarchy, offering it both praise and criticism.

According to recent reports, squid Game is still the most-viewed show in Netflix’s history in terms of raw viewership numbers, and it is hard to imagine anything catching up to it anytime soon. The series follows hundreds of financially desperate contestants who enter a secret competition built around deadly versions of children's games, with a life-changing cash prize waiting for the last survivor.

Sources indicate that A key array of factors helped Squid Game take advantage of a specific cultural moment and register with a substantial number of viewers; it aired towards the first wave of post-COVID reopenings when viewers were still used to binge-watching, resonated with an international audience at a time in which subtitles were becoming more accepted, and tapped into an “eat the rich” sentiment that had grown more prominent both in its production country of South Korea and its primary audience in the United States. Squid Game is a dark show that looks at the manipulation of the media from a cynical outlook, but the nature of the individual challenges is so entertaining that it also succeeds as a captivating thriller.

In a recent development, black Mirror is the heir apparent to The Twilight Zone as a science fiction anthology show that offered a variety of compelling stories about the near-future, but its perspective was far darker and more psychological. If The Twilight Zone often approached high-concept premises that had either a supernatural tilt or posed some sort of outstanding ethical debate, Black Mirror was a grave warning about the rapid accumulation of technology that also revealed the inherent cruelty of mankind.

In a recent development, black Mirror was the perfect show for a Netflix audience because each episode was standalone (outside of a few crossover events), allowing for certain episodes to rise above the rest and peak in viewership. The best thing about Black Mirror is that there is no strict definition of what it has to be or what rules it needs to abide by, which is why it is still an ongoing series with a ripe future in front of it.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

It has been revealed that you do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

Sources indicate that you are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

Recent findings suggest that you have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

It has been revealed that mindhunter is a two-season masterpiece created by David Fincher, the award-winning master filmmaker responsible for several of the greatest serial killer films ever made. Mindhunter is loosely based on the true story of the FBI Agent John Douglas, the real-life inspiration for the character of Will Graham in the Thomas Harris novels, and follows the FBI specialists Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) as they travel the country to interview famous serial killers and help local law enforcement officers solve particularly puzzling cases.

Recent findings suggest that mindhunter is sharp and stylized, exploring the nature of psychopathy in a way that has never been seen before, and it uses history to create deeply upsetting drama. Although the show was never picked up for a third season, likely because of the high price paid for its precision and attention to detail, it will go down in history as one of the greatest things that Fincher has ever made.

Narcos was one of the first highlights that proved that Netflix could produce hits that rivaled what could be seen on traditional networks, as the fact-based cartel thriller offered a riveting encapsulation of the history of the South American drug wars. Although Boyd Holbrook and Pedro Pascal made for a compelling set of protagonists who offered a perspective on what the DEA’s goals were during this period in history, Narcos was anchored by the brilliant performance of Wagner Moura as Pablo Escobar, as he was able to turn one of history’s greatest monsters into a nuanced anti-hero in the vein of Tony Soprano.

Narcos is a fascinating example of a series that was able to evolve and adapt over time, as it turned into a dense political drama in Season 2 before becoming a full-on espionage thriller in Season 3.

The Queen’s Gambit was a ministries phenomenon that became such a cultural event that it sparked a global rising interest in the art of chess, taking advantage of the game’s inherent dramatic power in a way that had never been captured before. Although anyone who is well-versed in chess knows that there is a very complex philosophy involved in strategy, The Queen’s Gambit matched that dynamic subject with a rich historical story about a complex anti-hero trapped in the midst of a historical period of siege and a personal battle with addiction.

Recent findings suggest that anya Taylor-Joy has already proven to be an exciting young actress based on her performances in Split and The Witch, but The Queen’s Gambit offered her the opportunity to give her best performance to date. It is one of the defining TV characters of the modern era, and one that it's impossible to imagine anyone else doing.

Industry observers note that ripley is hardly the first adaptation of the classic Patricia Highsmith novel The Talented Mr. Ripley, but showrunner Steve Zaillian reinterpreted the story in a fresh fresh way that stood as the most authentic to the book. Even if Ripley aged up the characters so that they would be older than they were in the novel, its use of stunning black-and-white imagery helped capture the noir spirit of a lonely, moody story about disenfranchisement among American expatriates living in Paris during the ‘60s.

Industry observers note that ripley is authentic to the source material in its decision to turn the titular anti-hero into a true cypher whose emotions are challenging to predict, as Andrew Scott was able to create a threatening, unsettling portrayal that was also strangely charismatic in a very unusual way. Rarely has a television show ever looked and felt so cinematic.

Adolescence is a great example of how Netflix can elevate a smaller-scale show and expose it to a much wider audience, as the series was so impactful that it might have caused change in the real world. The four-part series follows a 13-year-old boy accused of murdering a classmate, tracing the devastating impact of the case on his family while examining the influences that may have shaped his behavior.

Recent findings suggest that stephen Graham developed a highly emotional, challenging exploration of gender roles and the use of social media among children that led to global conversations about enacting change so that the type of violence that the show depicted could be avoided in the future. Adolescence walks a very tight line of being authentic in its exploration of relevant topics without being exploitative, and it was undoubtedly a positive move for Netflix to release a show that inspired such debate. It is hardly an easy watch, but one that would almost feel necessary in this day and age.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's officially the end of the road for The Last of Us at HBO. While the upcoming third season was already set to conclude the show's adaptation of the second game in Naughty Dog's acclaimed PlayStation series, there was some hope it could continue on after. Those hopes have now been squashed by HBO's boss.

Casey Bloys, chairman and CEO of HBO and Max content, shared several updates on upcoming projects with Deadline in September, following a successful night at the Emmys for the firm. That included The Last of Us, with Bloys saying that, "Craig [Mazin] has planned it as the final season.".

Mazin is the co-creator and showrunner of the series. After The Last of Us, he's moving on to create a Dungeons & Dragons show, a sequel to Baldur's Gate 3, for HBO.

After adapting the first game in the first season of the show, HBO split The Last of Us Part 2 across two seasons to reflect the game's dual protagonists. Season 2 tells the story of Ellie's (Bella Ramsey) quest for revenge following the death of Joel (Pedro Pascal) and her hunt for Abby (Kaitlyn Dever). Season 3 will flip the perspective, retelling the same period of time as season 2 from Abby's point of view. This will also introduce the character of Lev, played by Michelle Mao.

Neil Druckmann, co-creator of the game series, co-created the HBO show alongside Mazin. Druckmann served as a showrunner and writer for the first two seasons but stepped away from work on season 3. Recently he has continued to distance himself and Naughty Dog from the show, especially after the response to the second season was less than stellar. In a recent interview with The Washington Post, he affirmed that Naughty Dog had no creative role in the final season before teasing that he still has prepares for the future of the franchise.

As for when season 3 of the show will actually be released, Bloys reiterated that it is scheduled for 2027. He didn't give further details on a specific date or window beyond that. Don't worry though, as Sony is currently working on a God of War series for Prime Video starring Dave Bautista. The hunger for more game adaptations will be sated.

9 Cult Classic Crime Movies Where The Villain Is More Compelling Than The Hero

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes, no matter how dynamic a protagonist is, the villain still steals the show.
  • Industry observers note that it’s particularly true of cult crime movies, where filmmakers often explore the psychology of criminals rather than presenting straightforward good versus evil narratives.
  • According to recent reports, some are larger-than-life personalities who dominate every scene, while others are quietly unsettling precisely because their motivations remain so difficult to understand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes, no matter how dynamic a protagonist is, the villain still steals the show. A great crime movie understands that a fascinating adversary is just as compelling as the hero, particularly if the criminal has the right personality, philosophy, or sheer screen presence. In many crime movies, the main character's determination to uphold the law makes them somewhat predictable. The person they're chasing, on the other hand, can be driven by something far more unusual.

Industry observers note that it’s particularly true of cult crime movies, where filmmakers often explore the psychology of criminals rather than presenting straightforward good versus evil narratives. Their antagonists can be charismatic, unpredictable, frighteningly intelligent, or even strangely sympathetic, making it difficult to look away whenever they appear.

According to recent reports, some are larger-than-life personalities who dominate every scene, while others are quietly unsettling precisely because their motivations remain so difficult to understand. The heroes might provide the narrative's perspective, but it's the villains who give these crime classics much of their personality.

Martin Scorsese's remake of Cape Fear features Robert De Niro in one of his most flamboyant performances. He plays Max Cady, a newly released prisoner determined to exact revenge on Sam Bowden (Nick Nolte), the lawyer whose deliberately inadequate defense helped secure his conviction. De Niro makes Cady an almost cartoonishly theatrical psychopath while still being absolutely terrifying.

It has been revealed that he is also compellingly motivated to expose the hypocrisy beneath Bowden's respectable suburban life. Although Nolte gives an excellent performance, his lawyer is compromised by infidelity and professional dishonesty. Cady, meanwhile, understands precisely how to exploit those weaknesses. His extraordinary encounter with Bowden's teenage daughter Danielle (Juliette Lewis), in which he poses as her drama teacher, is particularly unsettling.

Sources indicate that scorsese's Cape Fear deliberately complicates the original’s straightforward distinction between an innocent family and a dangerous criminal. Cady might be monstrous, but Bowden is hardly the uncomplicated hero he initially appears to be.

Outstanding crime thriller To Live and Die in L.A. benefits greatly from having the perpetually scene-stealing Willem Dafoe as its antagonist. Dafoe plays Rick Masters, an exceptionally talented counterfeiter whose criminal operation attracts the attention of reckless Secret Service agent Richard Chance (William Petersen).

Chance is an entertaining protagonist, but his increasingly questionable methods make him difficult to distinguish from the criminals he pursues, particularly when he resorts to armed robbery to finance an undercover operation. Masters, by comparison, possesses an unusual combination of artistic ambition, professional discipline, and cold-blooded ruthlessness.

He’s an artist that approaches counterfeiting as a creative discipline, taking enormous pride in reproducing currency with extraordinary precision. To Live And Die In LA is particularly interested in the similarities between Masters and Chance, but Dafo gave Masters so much personality that the Chance simply cannot match him.

Sources indicate that 1990s classic Point Break stars Patrick Swayze as Bodhi, the charismatic leader of a gang of surfers who finance their endless summer by robbing banks while wearing masks of former American presidents. Keanu Reeves, meanwhile, plays Johnny Utah, an FBI agent who infiltrates the group and gradually becomes fascinated by its unconventional leader.

According to recent reports, bodhi is undoubtedly a criminal, but Swayze gives him an infectious enthusiasm that makes his philosophy surprisingly persuasive. He believes that society's obsession with money and conventional responsibilities prevents people from experiencing life fully.

Bodhi presents himself as a spiritual free spirit, but his supposed rejection of materialism is financed by stealing from other people. His philosophy is therefore considerably more selfish than he would like to admit. Nevertheless, Johnny's attraction to Bodhi is entirely understandable. Bodhi is the existential hero of the film, while Johnny is busy struggling to understand what he actually wants from life.

According to recent reports, ben Kingsley's performance as Don Logan in Sexy Beast is so extraordinary that it almost overwhelms the entire film. Playing a volatile London gangster sent to persuade retired criminal Gary “Gal” Dove (Ray Winstone) to participate in another robbery, Kingsley creates one of British cinema's most memorable villains.

According to recent reports, logan doesn't behave like the stereotypical cinematic gangster flaunting his wealth and luxury. Instead, he's a deeply unpleasant, psychologically manipulative bully whose entire personality seems designed to make everybody around him uncomfortable. Kingsley's performance is remarkable for its physical intensity. His rigid posture, piercing stare, clipped delivery, and sudden explosions of anger make even apparently ordinary conversations feel dangerous.

Industry observers note that he doesn't need to reach for a weapon to dominate a room because his greatest talent is making everybody else feel completely powerless. Gal is physically imposing but emotionally exhausted, and Gal's attempts to avoid violence make him increasingly vulnerable to Logan's bullying.

Industry observers note that christopher Walken gives one of his finest performances in Abel Ferrara's King of New York, playing Frank White, a powerful drug lord who returns to the city after serving a prison sentence. Although White is responsible for considerable violence, he also has an almost messianic vision of himself as somebody capable of transforming New York through his criminal wealth.

He genuinely seems to believe that his generosity somehow compensates for the brutality required to maintain his position. This contradiction gives the character a fascinating complexity, particularly because Walken never plays him as somebody who recognizes the absurdity of his own moral reasoning.

According to recent reports, walken's distinctive screen presence is essential to the character's appeal. White is remarkably calm, often speaking in a soft, almost hypnotic voice even when surrounded by people who would happily kill him. Walken's unusual delivery makes his occasional moments of violence particularly startling. The police officers pursuing him, particularly David Caruso's Dennis Gilley, provide a more conventional heroic perspective, but White is a much more intriguing figure because his ambitions extend beyond simple criminal survival.

Manhunter introduces audiences to cinema’s first Hannibal Lecter (Brian Cox), but its most compelling villain is arguably Francis Dollarhyde (Tom Noonan), the serial killer pursued by FBI profiler Will Graham (William Petersen). Known as the Tooth Fairy, Dollarhyde murders entire families while attempting to transform himself into the terrifying figure depicted in William Blake's painting The Great Red Dragon and the Woman Clothed with the Sun.

While Graham’s investigative abilities make him an interesting protagonist, Dollarhyde is the more fascinating character because Manhunter devotes considerable attention to the psychological damage underlying his disturbing behavior.

His relationship with Reba McClane (Joan Allen), a blind colleague at the film-processing laboratory where he works, gives him acceptance and intimacy for the first time. It's an unsettling contrast that makes him surprisingly sympathetic. Noonan's restraint makes Dollarhyde especially disturbing, giving Manhunter a villain whose vulnerability is every bit as unsettling as his violence.

According to recent reports, the Hitcher manages to make Rutger Hauer's villain utterly compelling without really providing any information about him. Hauer plays John Ryder, a mysterious hitchhiker picked up by young driver Jim Halsey (C. Thomas Howell) during a journey across the American Southwest. Almost immediately, Ryder reveals that he's a murderous psychopath, and Jim finds himself caught in an increasingly terrifying game of survival.

Industry observers note that ryder offers no conventional explanation for his behavior, not interested in money, revenge, or any other familiar criminal motivation. Instead, he seems to derive satisfaction from tormenting Jim, repeatedly appearing wherever the unfortunate young driver happens to be.

Sources indicate that hauer's performance makes this lack of explanation considerably more effective. He can be perfectly charming one moment and extraordinarily cruel the next. Although Howell effectively conveys Jim’s growing desperation, the character is deliberately less psychologically complicated than Ryder. Even when his behavior becomes completely reprehensible, it's difficult to look away.

True Romance features several memorable criminals, but Gary Oldman's Drexl Spivey is arguably the most entertaining. Playing a pimp and drug dealer who becomes involved in the increasingly dangerous circumstances surrounding Clarence Worley (Christian Slater), Oldman delivers a wonderfully eccentric performance that makes an enormous impression despite having relatively little screen time.

True Romance also boasts Christopher Walken as mobster Vincenzo Coccotti. His interrogation of Clarence's father, Clifford (Dennis Hopper), is one of the film's finest scenes, largely because Walken plays the character with such unnerving restraint. He allows an apparently casual conversation to become increasingly uncomfortable before revealing his true intentions.

Both performances illustrate the film's strength as a crime story populated by distinctive personalities. Clarence and Alabama (Patricia Arquette) provide its romantic center, but the criminals surrounding them supply much of its dark humor and unpredictability.

Although Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight is a superhero film, its structure and organized crime narrative make it one of the most compelling crime thrillers of the 21st century. Heath Ledger's Joker is the obvious highlight, delivering a performance so commanding that Christian Bale's Batman frequently feels like a supporting character in his own film.

Unlike conventional criminal masterminds, Joker is completely disinterested in accumulating wealth or establishing a sustainable criminal empire. He initially presents himself as somebody attempting to take control of Gotham's criminal underworld, but his real ambition is to demonstrate that society's moral principles are much more fragile than people would like to believe.

Bruce Wayne believes that his mission is ultimately about protecting Gotham's citizens and preserving their faith in justice. The Joker wants to demonstrate that those principles disappear when ordinary people are placed under sufficient pressure. The two-ferry experiment is the clearest expression of this philosophy. Ledger's Oscar-winning performance makes that absence of conventional crime movie motive all the more fascinating.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More spoilery than spoilers. This article contains, you guessed it, spoilers for "Blade Runner 2099.".

After two movies, several short films, the anime show "Black Lotus," and numerous novels and comics, how many directions are left to take the "Blade Runner" franchise? Well, that's easy. You simply go back to the original source material. "Blade Runner 2099" creator and showrunner Silka Luisa embraced the tall task of picking up the classic story where previous media left off — by going straight to the book that inspired it all.

In a recent development, those who've read Philip K. Dick's "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" will recognize the author's fingerprints all over the Mercerism plotline that rises to the fore late in "Blade Runner 2099." In the novel, this idiosyncratic religion centers on Wilber Mercer, a holy figure who climbs a mountain on a pilgrimage. The catch is, he does so while having rocks thrown at him mercilessly, inspiring the idea to recreate his torturous ascent through a virtual reality device known as an empathy box. This was one of the biggest aspects that both "Blade Runner" movies completely skipped, preferring to focus on the more grounded details of this cyberpunk world while eschewing the spiritual.

That finally changes here, as I discussed with Luisa during a press junket. "I was always fascinated by Mercerism," she explained. "Just the idea that there was a religion that was technology-based where people would be completely isolated, but then join through technology so that they could feel empathy with each other — that feels so current." She went on to theorize:.

It has been revealed that "If you sold [empathy boxes] today, I genuinely think people would buy them. There is this deep longing for connection, and we no longer know how to get in a room and be with each other.".

Given the digital horrors we've normalized on an everyday basis in recent years (the impending threat of a superintelligence bent on our destruction, generative AI, and the ever-present hellscape that is social media), it's not too much of a leap to take "Blade Runner 2099" creator Silka Luisa at her word about Mercerism. Somewhere, there almost certainly would be a segment of the population all too happy to strap themselves into an empathy box device and electroshock themselves into feeling the same pain that Wilber Mercer supposedly did. (Of course, his entire ascent is eventually revealed to be a staged incident that never actually happened, but that's neither here nor there.).

But, even more than that unsettling hypothetical, Luisa had an even better reason to introduce the concept of Mercerism into "2099." As she excitedly told me:.

Sources indicate that "[...] Just from a creative and an imagination standpoint, it was so exciting to be like, 'Okay, I only have a couple words of description here, but what does an empathy box look like? How do we find references from the real-world that we can build out into it?'".

In the series, Michelle Yeoh's Replicant Olwen gets an up close and personal experience with an unfriendly Mercerite cultist. For Luisa, this provided a unique opportunity to flesh out what was in the scripts:.

"Trying to design the murals that are in the chapel, all the little paraphernalia that would go with it, who would be practitioners of it. That's just such fun world-building that, I mean, what other show are you gonna get to do that on?".

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" (you can read our review here) are now streaming on Prime Video.

‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs.
  • While a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients.
  • And yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her new friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

While a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

And yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

It has been revealed that “In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” said Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”.

According to recent reports, the scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her upcoming companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

It has been revealed that “I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” remarked Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”.

Hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

“The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very vital and really supports this scene,” said Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”.

One topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

Industry observers note that “I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” said Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”.

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi remarked no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”.

“There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

“For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very vital turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”.

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that pedro Pascal is one of the biggest, most in-demand actors in Hollywood right now. "The Mandalorian" star is as big as he's ever been, especially since he's part of the full cast of "Avengers: Doomsday," which arrives in December. He's reprising his role as Reed Richards from last year's "The Fantastic Four: First Steps." And yes, that's going to be a must-see cinematic event for people all over the world, but Pascal is starring in another movie that demands to be seen in theaters as well.

"Behemoth!" is not as big as "Doomsday." In fact, I'd go so far as to wager a lot of people reading this are probably hearing about it for the first time. It's a smaller drama that might not typically earn the "must-see in theaters" label in the streaming era. Be that as it may, it's absolutely worth prioritizing in theaters, as watching it at home is going to leave a whole lot to be desired in comparison.

Sources indicate that the movie focuses on a gifted cellist named Alex Serian (Pascal), who returns home to Los Angeles after 20 years on the road. Music completely consumes him, but a turn of events leads him on an unexpected journey that completely alters his life. That's the gist of it, without spoiling some of the more compelling details that are better discovered while watching the movie.

Tony Gilroy is the man who made "Andor" within the "Star Wars" galaxy, but he's also a very talented filmmaker outside of that franchise (see "Michael Clayton"). This represents his return to the director's chair for a feature film for the first time in 14 years. It's a very welcome one at that. It's also arguably Pascal's greatest performance to date in his impressive career. But none of those very good reasons to see this movie are why it demands to be seen in a theater.

It has been revealed that "Behomoth!" is a non-linear character study through the lens of a man's singular obsession with music and how that complicates his important relationships outside of that obsession. It's a f*****g good movie. But it's also very much a movie about music and the love of music, so it should come as no surprise that it also contains some incredible music. That's why this movie is so greatly enhanced by the theatrical experience.

I was lucky enough to catch this one at the Austin Film Festival this year, and from the opening scene, the swell of the orchestral arrangements hit me like a brick wall. With all due respect to the theater I was in, it's not like I was in a fancy IMAX auditorium or a decked out Dolby Cinema screen. It was just a damn good theater. But that made all of the difference.

Recent findings suggest that even as someone who cherishes the theatrical experience and considers himself a blockbuster junkie (as evidenced by my favorite movies of all time), this isn't the type of movie that I'd normally scream about needing to be seen in a theater. However, Tony Gilroy and the movie's wildly impressive list of composers, which includes everyone from Michael Giacchino to Alan Silvestri, outdid themselves. The sound hits you like a train, and no matter how good most people's home audio setup is, it's just not going to compare.

Industry observers note that "Trolls World Tour" was the least likely movie that changed Hollywood forever, making it possible to watch new releases at home. That coupled with the rise of streaming has made it easier than ever for people to stay home and watch movies. When they do go to theaters, it's not for "little" dramas like this. But this movie is absolutely a spectacle in its own way, making it worth seeking out.

Sources indicate that I'm not trying to lower one movie to raise the other. I'm going to see "Avengers: Doomsday" on opening night. I'm very excited about it. The "Avengers: Doomsday" ticket pre-sales have already topped the entire run of "Supergirl." That movie doesn't need anyone's help. Nobody needs to be told to get off the couch for that one.

"Behemoth!" is a movie that doesn't scream "must-see spectacle" on the surface. But the craft on display is enthralling, and the sound is nothing shy of a minor miracle of cinema. It's a love letter to music and a cautionary tale about obsession, with both sides of that coin benefitting marvelously from the experience that only a movie theater can offer. Watching movies at home has never been better, but it's still not quite the same thing.

Also, let me again remind you that Tony Gilroy made the modern masterpiece that is "Michael Clayton." That's absolutely the filmmaker who is back in the saddle for this one, alongside Pedro Pascal giving it all in a role that he was made for. The stars aligned for this one, and it's absolutely, rightfully going to be in the awards season conversation. But it's also at risk of being one of those movies that gets lost in the flow at the box office as bigger things surround it.

Sources indicate that I'm here to tell you this: "Behemoth!" is not a "wait to stream it" movie. No matter how it may look on the surface, this is precisely the kind of cinematic experience people claim to crave. Something original and worthy of leaving the house for. This is worth the time and money, even if it's not a $100 million blockbuster. It's spectacular in its own way.

"Behemoth!" hits theaters on December 4, 2026.

“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

Sources indicate that ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and major mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.” Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down.

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”.

The cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover new series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Big Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three latest series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

Deadline first reported the news.

  • Recent findings suggest that robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Recent findings suggest that robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly vital sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

It has been revealed that transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney.

Industry News: ​​Massive Changes Are Coming To The DC Universe In 2027

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that with James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future has never been more uncertain.
  • In a recent development, the 2020s have not been all that kind to DC's cinematic efforts.
  • In a recent development, fans gained renewed hope when Gunn and Safran were appointed co-heads of the newly-formed DC Studios in 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future has never been more uncertain. Their departure came in the wake of Paramount and Warner Bros merging under the Skydance banner, and substantial changes are now in the offing as CEO David Ellison prepares to reinvent DC yet again.

In a recent development, the 2020s have not been all that kind to DC's cinematic efforts. After a solid start to the DC Extended Universe (DCEU) with 2013's "Man of Steel," things slowly went off the rails, resulting in a sorry state of affairs in 2023 when the so-called Snyderverse delivered back-to-back flops that ultimately caused the entire enterprise to implode.

In a recent development, fans gained renewed hope when Gunn and Safran were appointed co-heads of the newly-formed DC Studios in 2022. The pair were supposed to be franchise saviors, rebooting DC and revitalizing its popularity among the masses. Unfortunately, while their vision of a DC Universe that spanned movies and TV got off to a decent enough start with Gunn's 2025 crowd-pleaser "Superman," chapter one of the DC Universe, titled "Gods and Monsters," has thus far failed to deliver any massive hits. Now, Ellison and his cohorts are faced with having to once again relaunch the DC franchise, and you can bet things are going to look a lot different.

Sources indicate that for now, it remains unclear exactly what Ellison and co. have in-store beyond installing newly introduced leadership and taking a long hard look at recent failures. But 2027 will undoubtedly bring major new developments and it's not hard to guess what they might be. Here's everything we can expect for the DC Universe in 2027.

It has been revealed that james Gunn and Peter Safran's DC departure isn't just about installing fresh leadership. Skydance CEO David Ellison reportedly wants to dismantle Gunn's universe entirely, marking what will almost certainly be the premature end of the Gods and Monsters chapter. Meanwhile, Ellison has installed a new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios as of December 1, 2026: Jeremy Latcham.

It has been revealed that who is Jeremy Latcham? He's a former Marvel Studios producer with a predilection for broad, family-friendly entertainment — so the opposite of a "Creature Commandos" series, animated movies based on two different Robins, and box office flops like "Supergirl." But it's not entirely clear how easy it will be for Ellison and Latcham to deconstruct Gunn's DC project. Dozens of projects are in production or early development, and in order to start from scratch, the new leadership would have to cancel all of them.

Industry observers note that that's obviously not going to happen. We already know Gunn is sticking around to finish his "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow," which is presently set for release on July 9, 2027. Meanwhile, Deadline has listed all the DC Universe projects currently in some stage of production and there's more than you'd think. Still, while it remains to be seen how Ellison and Latcham approach this, you can bet 2027 will bring several cancellations and likely several pivots, a là what happened to "Lanterns" when Gunn and Safran brought in Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof, and Tom King to replace Greg Berlanti, Marc Guggenheim, and Seth Grahame-Smith as lead creatives.

Recent findings suggest that for now, Latcham has a significant to-do list that includes scanning the existing projects already in production and deciding which ones can be jettisoned and which can't. We'll almost certainly hear news on that front next year.

One of Marvel Comics' best modern writers, "Secret Wars" author Jonatham Hickman, is a secret Marvel Cinematic Universe consultant, but things haven't quite worked that way on the DC side. A report from Bleeding Cool claimed that president, publisher, and chief creative officer of DC Comics, Jim Lee, had felt frozen out by James Gunn and Peter Safran, suggesting he had little to no input into plans for their DC Universe.

Sources indicate that now, however, news has emerged which bodes well for Lee's involvement in the cinematic side of DC going forward. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Skydance has made some major organizational changes that include bringing DC Comics under Skydance's products and publishing team. That means Lee — alongside executive vice president and general manager of DC Comics, Anne DePies — now reports to the head of that division, Josh Silverman. As THR notes, "DC Comics is an incubator for the characters and storylines that ultimately end up on screen," and Lee now conceivably has more of an opportunity to get involved in the DC Studios side of things.

In a memo to staff, acquired by THR, Silverman told employees Lee and DePies would continue "shaping the future of [DC's] iconic characters and enduring stories, and driving the growth and success of the brand across the studio." That certainly sounds like they'll be collaborating with others in the tech giant, though for now it remains unclear exactly how much they'll be working with Jeremy Latcham and the newly introduced DC Studios.

Newly introduced DC Studios head Jeremy Latcham co-produced some of the Marvel Cinematic Universe's biggest hits, including "Iron Man," "Spider-Man: Homecoming," and even James Gunn's own "Guardians of the Galaxy" (his post-Marvel output unfortunately includes one of the most forgettable movies of 2026: Nate Bargatze's "The Breadwinner"). Latcham has also made no secret of his desire to see more family-friendly movies being released (hopefully better ones than "The Breadwinner") and generally seems to be more inclined towards mass entertainment than Gunn.

When Latcham's DC appointment was first announced, much of the online discussion revolved around his prior approach to Marvel movies, which he explained as involving a "grandma test." This is essentially shorthand for Latcham trying to appeal to casual audiences. It should be said that, as the upcoming DC Studios president, Latcham is reporting to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein rather David Ellison himself, which means there's more oversight than in the Gunn/Safran era. But Latcham will surely be given freedom to pursue more projects with mass appeal.

Meanwhile, Ellison has a debt situation. Gunn and Safran's DC Studios exit was reportedly driven in part by cost-cutting. Skydance has $80 billion in debt, with Ellison promising to deliver $6 billion in yearly savings over the next three years. He needs massive blockbusters to do that, and Latcham has the experience necessary. As such, if DC does make any major announcements about forthcoming projects in 2027, expect them to be about marquee characters: Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman. Depending on how rapidly things move, we might even get some news about a Justice League movie — though given his experience at Marvel, Latcham might want to focus on establishing the characters in their own right before rushing into a team-up movie.

In a recent development, you can't rebuild a franchise without firing a few people, so brace for some major casting changes. So far, nothing has been made official but, based on the aforementioned considerations regarding big blockbusters with mass appeal, you can bet Jeremy Latcham will cast a new Batman soon. Robert Pattinson is already playing the character in Matt Reeves' "The Batman" movies, but those were designated "Elseworlds" projects and were entirely separate from James Gunn's DC Universe. With Pattinson leaving Batman for James Bond and Gunn out of the picture, Ellison and Latcham can finally give the people a new Batman — and have every incentive to do so ASAP.

Superman is trickier, as David Corenswet is set to reprise the role in "Man of Tomorrow." Whether he'll stick around after that is unclear, but if Latcham does decide to recast, we might not hear about it until late 2027, or possibly even 2028.

Sources indicate that whether people like "Lanterns" star Aaron Pierre, who played John Stewart in the HBO series, will stay put is less obvious. The actor addressed the matter during a November 2026 appearance on the IndieWire: Screen Talk podcast, saying, "My relationship with James and my relationship with Peter is a beautiful relationship," adding, "What happens beyond this point is not my decision. So I'm very at peace [...] what will be will be." While it's not entirely clear what the new DC Studios leadership has planned, then, you can bet there'll be some major casting news in 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that one of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone.

  • It has been revealed that earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that one of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation.

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, Newly introduced Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

In a recent development, and in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

According to recent reports, and for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Industry observers note that whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

8 Perfect Thriller Books That Pretty Much Anyone Can Enjoy

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that who doesn't love a good thriller?
  • If you're looking for a mystery or suspenseful story to dive into, the titles below have you covered.
  • Industry observers note that "All conflict can be traced back to someone's feelings getting hurt, don't you think?" This bestseller spawned a star-studded TV show as well as a sequel published earlier this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that who doesn't love a good thriller? When handled right, it's one of the most entertaining genres in fiction. That noted, there are only a select few thrillers with true broad appeal. They're so good, so gripping and strongly written, that almost anyone will be hooked from the opening pages.

If you're looking for a mystery or suspenseful story to dive into, the titles below have you covered. They run the gamut from sun-drenched psychological battles and dark character studies to tangled domestic dramas and gripping real-life investigations.

Industry observers note that "All conflict can be traced back to someone's feelings getting hurt, don't you think?" This bestseller spawned a star-studded TV show as well as a sequel published earlier this year. Big Little Lies follows three women, Madeline, Celeste, and Jane, whose children attend the same primary school. Their lives are complicated by marital difficulties, schoolyard rivalries, and long-buried secrets, which begin to boil over after someone is killed during a school fundraising event (though the victim's identity is kept from the reader).

That's a juicy mystery to keep us hooked, and author Liane Moriarty fills it out with relatable domestic drama, sharp social satire, a welcome touch of dark humor, and a cast of flawed characters. They're all intense but believable, with their petty arguments and insecurities providing plenty of entertainment even when the central mystery temporarily takes a back seat.

"Intelligence work has one moral law: it is justified by results." One of the most influential spy stories ever, offering a grimly realistic alternative to the glamorous adventures of James Bond. Set during the Cold War, The Spy Who Came in from the Cold centers on Alec Leamas, a disillusioned British intelligence officer whose network of agents in East Germany has been systematically destroyed. With his career seemingly approaching its conclusion, Leamas agrees to undertake one final mission to undermine a powerful East German intelligence official.

Industry observers note that however, the operation involves an elaborate deception, forcing Leamas to navigate a dangerous world where loyalties are uncertain and practically everyone has something to hide. However, the tale that follows doesn't rely on fancy gadgets or spectacular action sequences. Instead, it's more psychological, leaning into moral complexity and a three-dimensional protagonist.

"To be a human is complex, and often painful." This atmospheric mystery is set in the Adirondack Mountains, where a teenager named Barbara Van Laar disappears from a summer camp in 1975. She belongs to the wealthy family that owns the camp, and her disappearance is particularly disturbing because her older brother, Bear, vanished from the same property fourteen years earlier. From there, the novel moves between different time periods and shifts between various characters, all of them exceptionally well-developed.

Sources indicate that in the process, we gradually piece together the complicated history of the Van Laar family and the people whose lives have become entangled with theirs. There is social commentary and subtext here, but it's never heavy-handed or elevated above the mystery itself. Not to mention, the setting is immersive and memorable, vividly recreating the '70s and transporting us to an ominous, forested world.

"Beauty is terror. Whatever we call beautiful, we quiver before it." The Secret History is an extraordinary literary thriller, delivering both suspenseful and sharp psychological insight. The main character is Richard Papen, a young Californian who enrolls at an exclusive Vermont college and becomes involved with a small group of eccentric classics students. However, their intellectual pursuits eventually lead to a horrifying crime, followed by another murder that Richard reveals in the novel's opening pages.

Here, author Donna Tartt creates an intoxicating atmosphere of intellectual ambition and moral decay, all of it unfolding against a darkly cozy backdrop of fire-lit common rooms and ornate old buildings. (In this regard, the book is a cornerstone of the 'dark academia' subgenre.) The characters are impressively realistic, and the writing itself is great the whole way through, pulling the reader from page to page.

"The Thames is a tidal river, its powerful currents ebbing and surging twice each day with salt water from the North Sea." This is a work of nonfiction, but it's more gripping than pretty much any fictional thriller published this year. London Falling explores the mysterious death of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a luxury London apartment in 2019. Following his death, Zac's devastated parents begin investigating the circumstances surrounding his final hours, gradually discovering that their son had been leading a secret life.

He had reinvented himself as the wealthy heir to a Russian oligarch, using his fabricated identity to infiltrate London's exclusive social circles. Writer Patrick Radden Keefe undertakes a brave, dogged search for the truth, in the process profiling a collection of criminals, socialites, unreliable witnesses, and violent men.​​​​ However, the book's emotional center remains Zac's parents.

In a recent development, "There's a difference between really loving someone and loving the idea of her." While David Fincher's film adaptation is widely accepted as a modern classic, Gillian Flynn's original Gone Girl novel is fantastic, too, and worth reading if you're a big fan of the movie. When Amy Dunne mysteriously disappears, her husband, Nick, becomes the prime suspect, particularly as evidence emerges suggesting that their marriage was far from happy.

The novel alternates between Nick's account of the investigation and entries from Amy's diary.
